、动力系统方向；数学物理方向；应用数学方向；概率统计方向。其中，代数与数论、数学物理以及动力系统与随机分析这三个科研团队，已达到世界顶尖水平。 代数、代数几何、数论方向 研究课题涉及表示论、代数几何、数论中的多个重要研究领域。研究方向包括代数表示理论、几何表示理论与范畴化，I-adic上同调理论及其应用、模空间、Hodge理论、奇点理论、算术代数几何等。 组长：朱艺航 副组长：李鹏辉 几何拓扑方向研究课题覆盖的方向较全面，如微分几何、几何分析、Teichmüller 理论、低维拓扑、高维流形拓扑、复几何等。 组长： 林剑锋 副组长： 高鸿灏 教授： 丘成桐、Kenji Fukaya、Akito Futaki、林勇、Vladimir Markovic、吴云辉 副教授：林剑锋、肖建、高鸿灏 助理教授：陈伟彦、孙巍峰、朱波、朱知非 博士后：Choudhury Diptaishik、Shanon Rubin、樊双赫、何翔、胡家昊、牛唯喆、青成昊、王大洵、刘洋、康凡、粟文泽、Benjamin Yamin Zhou、 Dang Quang Tuan 、池文豪、张筱筱、顾坪昕、胡春阳、Thomas Rodewald 分析、PDE、动力系统方向 分析、PDE、动力系统研究有限维和无限维状态空间随定律的时间演化。历史上，对这些问题的研究与数学其它学科的发展联系密切，研究中需要运用分析、拓扑、群论等方法，不少数学理论在这些问题的研究基础上发展起来。研究方向有：动力系统、相对论与波方程、流体力学、椭圆偏微分方程、拟随机群和Cayley图等。 组长：王学成 副组长：荆文甲 教授：陈志杰、 张翼华 副教授：金龙、荆文甲 、王学成 助理教授：归斌、兰洋、张城、李力、张景宣 博士后：Artiles Calix Albert Alejandro、张世红、Kumar Pranav、Biswas Debam、崔翰、龙辰纲 数学物理方向 数学物理是数学和物理的交叉领域，应用特定的数学方法来研究物理学的某些部分。也利用物理学的方法计算数学中的对象。数学和物理学的发展，历史上一直密不可分，许多数学理论是在物理问题的基础上发展起来的，很多数学方法和工具通常也只在物理学中找到实际应用。主要研究方向：超弦理论，量子引力，规范/引力对偶、超对称场论及其在几何中的应用、范畴论与凝聚态物理中的拓扑序等。 组长：宋伟 副组长：周杰 教授： David、Nikolaos Angelinos、Sarthak Duary、Singh Rahul、Galviz Blanco Daniel Eduardo、陈良玉、靳安然、阮钰泽、邵钰菓、许容阁、潘俏尹、葛东胜、魏付川、赵子烁、杨培赫、冯凌璇 弦论研究团队 https://ymsc-strings.github.io/seminar.html 应用数学方向 计算和应用数学关注使用数学理论和方法来解决实际问题，以及通过数值方法对数学模型进行计算和分析。这一领域涵盖了诸如数学建模、数值分析、优化、反问题、数据科学、密码学等多个子领域，被广泛应用于工程、物理、经济、金融、生物学等多个学科。计算和应用数学不仅提供工具来近似解决复杂的数学问题，同时也为各领域的科学研究和工程实践提供了坚实的理论支撑。主要研究方向包括：后量子密码学、数学建模、数值分析、偏微分方程数值解、计算动力系统、数值代数、反问题、图像处理、大规模优化方法、材料科学的数学理论与计算、应用分析、机器学习理论、运营和收益管理理论。 统计学是数据科学的基础，也是其核心组成部分之一。它是关于数据收集、数据分析、解释及推断的理论和方法的学问，并广泛用于科学、工程、医学、金融、政府管理等等领域，获取各种数据背后的信息、规律以及对其不确定性进行可靠的勾画，并以此对未来进行相对准确的预测。主要研究方向包括：因果推断、缺失数据、模型选择和平均、多臂老虎机、高维数据和机器学习等。 组长：杨宇红 副组长：杨帆(男) 教授： Per Register Paper locations have been assigned, authors can now register: Author Registration Information Paper presentation preferences emails to Authors have been sent, responses are due by Sept. 30 AOE The Career site is open See this blog post for details on the registration process Aug 25, 2026: NeurIPS has no affiliation or partnership with any third-party service that claims to collect registration or housing information on our behalf. The only authorized source for NeurIPS registration and Housing is through the official NeurIPS website. Please do not share registration details with any outside party. July 23, 2026: Due to a technical issue during release, we are currently re-releasing all reviews and initial meta-reviews. Reviews will be temporarily offline during that time. AI Reviewing Experiment This year NeurIPS will be held in Sydney, Atlanta, and Paris. Author Eligibility. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The responsibility for that error is ours as an organization, and we deeply apologize for the alarm and impact this miscommunication had on our community. We have updated the link and clarified the text of our policy, which is consistent with that of ACM and IEEE, as well as other international conferences and NeurIPS in the past. As in previous years, NeurIPS welcomes submissions from all compliant institutions and individuals. We want to reiterate that NeurIPS is a community-driven event, created by and for the community, and strives to be inclusive. The NeurIPS 2026 organizing committee was particularly saddened to learn of this institutional miscommunication. Register Paper locations have been assigned, authors can now register: Author Registration Information Paper presentation preferences emails to Authors have been sent, responses are due by Sept. 30 AOE The Career site is open See this blog post for details on the registration process Aug 25, 2026: NeurIPS has no affiliation or partnership with any third-party service that claims to collect registration or housing information on our behalf. The only authorized source for NeurIPS registration and Housing is through the official NeurIPS website. Please do not share registration details with any outside party. July 23, 2026: Due to a technical issue during release, we are currently re-releasing all reviews and initial meta-reviews. Reviews will be temporarily offline during that time. AI Reviewing Experiment This year NeurIPS will be held in Sydney, Atlanta, and Paris. Author Eligibility. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The responsibility for that error is ours as an organization, and we deeply apologize for the alarm and impact this miscommunication had on our community. We have updated the link and clarified the text of our policy, which is consistent with that of ACM and IEEE, as well as other international conferences and NeurIPS in the past. As in previous years, NeurIPS welcomes submissions from all compliant institutions and individuals. We want to reiterate that NeurIPS is a community-driven event, created by and for the community, and strives to be inclusive. The NeurIPS 2026 organizing committee was particularly saddened to learn of this institutional miscommunication. The organizing committee has taken on the responsibility of running the conference this year with the goal of fostering open communication, knowledge sharing, and global scientific discourse. We thank the community for bringing this issue to our attention and working with us through this situation. ICLR is globally renowned for presenting and publishing cutting-edge research on all aspects of deep learning used in the fields of artificial intelligence, statistics and data science, as well as important application areas such as machine vision, computational biology, speech recognition, text understanding, gaming, and robotics. ICLR is one of the fastest growing artificial intelligence conferences in the world. Participants at ICLR span a wide range of backgrounds, from academic and industrial researchers, to entrepreneurs and engineers, to graduate students and postdocs. The rapidly developing field of deep learning is concerned with questions surrounding how we can best learn meaningful and useful representations of data. ICLR takes a broad view of the field and includes topics such as feature learning, metric learning, compositional modeling, structured prediction, reinforcement learning, and issues regarding large-scale learning and non-convex optimization. A non-exhaustive list of relevant topics explored at the conference include: Unsupervised, Semi-supervised, and Supervised Representation Learning Representation Learning for Planning and Reinforcement Learning Metric Learning and Kernel Learning Sparse Coding and Dimensionality Expansion Hierarchical Models Optimization for Representation Learning Learning Representations of Outputs or States Implementation Issues, Parallelization, Software Platforms, Hardware Applications in Vision, Audio, Speech, Natural Language Processing, Robotics, Neuroscience, or Any Other Field

items.title: Commission seeks feedback on advertising repositories under the Digital Services Act
items.summary: Today, the European Commission is calling for evidence to gather feedback on upcoming technical guidelines concerning advertising repositories under the Digital Services Act (DSA). These enable that information about ads is available to the public and easy to access. Once adopted, the guidelines will aim to ensure that the advertising repositories provided by very large online platforms (VLOPs) and very large online search engines (VLOSEs) are effective. The Commission invites responses from a range of experts, including researchers, civil society organisations, journalists, providers of VLOPs/VLOSEs, and representatives from the advertising industry. These responses will help to shape the guidelines. Advertising repositories enable researchers, civil society, journalists and national authorities to detect risks related to online advertising, including online scams, disinformation campaigns, misleading commercial practices and the promotion of illegal products and services, among other

The Commission invites responses from a range of experts, including researchers, civil society organisations, journalists, providers of VLOPs/VLOSEs, and representatives from the advertising industry. items.title: Call for Proposals: PyTorch Day China 2026
items.summary: The Call for Proposals for PyTorch Day China 2026 closes November 10 at 23:59 China Standard Time . The event takes place in Beijing on December 12 , bringing together PyTorch developers, machine learning engineers, AI researchers, and open source AI leaders from across China and beyond. The call welcomes session presentations and lightning talks across five topic areas: Model Training & Post-Training : Distributed training, SFT, reinforcement learning, preference optimization, and techniques for improving training efficiency and performance. Efficient Inference & Deployment : LLM inference, quantization, optimization, deployment strategies, and production-ready AI solutions. PyTorch Core & Hardware Acceleration : Compilation, kernel optimization, performance profiling, and GPU and AI accelerator technologies. Physical AI : Robotics, intelligent devices, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, perception and control systems, and simulation-based training. PyTorch Ecosystem & Applications

items.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
items.summary: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports
items.content: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. Spotlight: Microsoft research newsletter Microsoft Research Newsletter Stay connected to the research community at Microsoft. Subscribe today Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush. How to use 1. Use Flint in your chat Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation. Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns. 2. Build an interactive app with Flint Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas. Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa. 3. Create bespoke interactions To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks. Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes. How it works Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level: Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates. Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states. Figure 1: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable c and cost effective. This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards. Try it now! Video playback requires cookie consent Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery. App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab) . Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app. Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab) , design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary. items.raw_text: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. items.content: Algorithms and theory Google’s mission presents many exciting algorithmic and optimization challenges across different product areas including Search, Ads, Social, and Google Infrastructure. These include optimizing internal systems such as scheduling the machines that power the numerous computations done each day, as well as optimizations that affect core products and users, from online allocation of ads to page-views to automatic management of ad campaigns, and from clustering large-scale graphs to finding best paths in transportation networks. Other than employing new algorithmic ideas to impact millions of users, Google researchers contribute to the state-of-the-art research in these areas by publishing in top conferences and journals. Recent Publications See More Depth-CoT Tradeoffs in Transformers: A Look at Path Following Clayton Sanford Matus Telgarsky Justin D. Li 2027 Preview Preview abstract Modern transformers have been scaled up in size, data, training-time compute, and more recently test-time compute based on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the consequences of trading off these parameters are unknown. We construct explicit tradeoffs between two of these aspects: the number of layers in a transformer and the number of CoT tokens. Our first result is general: with mild assumptions and a single-token prompt, for any integer k, a transformer using soft attention and SwiGLU MLP layers with L layers and n CoT tokens can be converted to a transformer with at most ckL layers and ⌈n/k⌉ CoT tokens, and vice versa, although with an increase to the size of other parameters. We then a multi-token prompt path following task, finding that additional preprocessing from the multi-token prompt changes the depth-CoT relationship in this case. We construct an attention-only network with L layers and 2^(L−2) heads that can traverse 2^(L−1) − 1 edges along a path with a single CoT token, demonstrating at least an exponential relationship between increases in depth and reductions in the number of CoT tokens needed to traverse the entire path. This relationship for the path following task holds empirically as well, as demonstrated by training networks with up to 5 layers, with the tradeoff between depth and the maximum number of edge traversals in a single CoT token exactly matching our theoretical constructions. View details A simple and efficient implementation of strong call by need by an abstract machine Małgorzata Biernacka Witold Charatonik Tomasz Drab Journal of Functional Programming, Volume 36 (2026) Preview Preview abstract We present an abstract machine for a strong call-by-need strategy in the lambda calculus. The machine has been derived automatically from a higher-order evaluator that uses the technique of memothunks to implement laziness. The derivation has been done with the use of an off-the-shelf transformation tool implementing the "functional correspondence" between higher-order interpreters and abstract machines, and it yields a simple and concise description of the machine. We prove that the resulting machine conservatively extends the lazy version of Krivine machine for the weak call-by-need strategy, and that it simulates the normal-order strategy in bilinear number of steps. View details Marginalized Bundle Adjustment: Multi-View Camera Pose from Monocular Depth Estimates Shengjie Zhu Ahmed Abdelkader Mark Matthews Xiaoming Liu Vincent Chu International Conference on 3D Vision (2026) Preview Preview abstract Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a classical 3D vision task for recovering camera parameters and scene geometry from multi-view images. Recent advances in deep learning enable accurate monocular depth estimation (MDE) that infers structure from a single image without depending on camera motion. But integrating MDE into SfM remains challenging. Unlike classical triangulated sparse pointclouds, MDE produces dense depthmaps with significantly higher error variance. Inspired by modern RANSAC estimators, we propose a Marginalized Bundle Adjustment (MBA) to accommodate MDE error variance with its density. With MBA, we show that MDE depthmaps are sufficiently accurate to support SoTA or competitive results in Structure-from-Motion and camera relocalization. Our benchmark demonstrates consistent remarkable results from two-view, few-frames small multiview, to thousands-frames large multiview system. Our method highlights the significant potential of MDE on multi-view 3D vision tasks. View details Cardio Load in exercise and everyday life: A modified TRIMP metric for continuously-sensing consumer wearables Justin Phillips Daniel Roggen YongSuk Cho Robert Harle Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise (2026) Preview Preview abstract PURPOSE: To introduce Cardio Load (CL), a metric quantifying cardiovascular work from all activities across the day, and to investigate its distribution by age, gender, and workout profiles. CL adapts the Training Impulse (TRIMP) model by leveraging continuous heart rate and movement data from wearables, enabling minute-level intensity estimation. We also discuss the derivation of weekly target loads, intended to guide fitness maintenance. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 31.2 million hours of wrist-worn wearable data collected over a six-week period. The dataset comprised a 40,000-subject subset (37.9% female) of consenting Google Pixel Watch® users in the United States, aged 18 to 80 years (18-39: 41.8%, 40-59: 43.5%, 60+: 14.6%). Measured data included minute-interval heart rate averages, resting and maximum heart rates, minute-interval averaged accelerometer log energy, and manually-logged or auto-detected activity types. Cardio Load scores and target loads were calculated daily for each subject and compared across age and gender. We also compared the proportions of CL gained during workouts and incidental daily activities for these groups. RESULTS: Overall, the study population's mean ± SD weekly CL scores were 221 ± 156 (female) and 259 ± 169 (male). Median weekly Cardio Load (CL) values exhibited consistency for individuals between 30 and 75 years of age. When analyzed in five-year age groups, the coefficient of variation (CV%) of median weekly CL values within this age range was less than 4.5%, with younger and older subjects demonstrating higher and lower median CL, respectively. The median proportion of CL accumulated during structured workouts versus incidental daily activity was 41.0% (female) and 49.0% (male) for all subjects, though this varied considerably with average weekly workout duration. CV% of weekly target load and daily target load over 6 weeks was 23.6% and 35.2% respectively. CONCLUSION: Cardio Load provides a continuous quantification of activity load from wearables, acknowledging both structured workouts and everydayincidental activity. CL is equitably rewarded for age ranges spanning 30-75 years. Weekly target loads were found to have little measurement variability and be more consistent and, consequently, more practical for planning training and physical activity than daily targets. View details Surviving the perfect storm: how hardware PMs can beat the AI tax and trade tariffs Akash Rathi Mind The Product (2026) Preview Preview abstract This piece analyzes how hardware product managers can navigate the financial pressure of AI-related costs and trade tariffs. It presents a practical framework for deploying the Joint Development Model (JDM) as a product development strategy to balance innovation with cost efficiency, enabling sustainable growth for next-generation AI-native consumer devices. View details Geo-Contextual AI Concierge: Minimizing Internal Support Friction Through Proactive Knowledge Synthesis Neeraj Choudhary Dónal Doyle Technical Report (2026) Preview Preview abstract In large-scale distributed enterprises, traditional Knowledge Management (KM) systems face a critical failure mode: static documentation cannot keep pace with evolving operational realities and regional nuances. This "knowledge latency" forces employees out of self-service workflows and into costly support ticketing queues. This paper introduces SENTINEL, a geo-contextual AI framework designed to shift enterprise support from reactive retrieval to proactive interception. The architecture employs a novel dual-engine system integrated into an omni-present interface. The first engine utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct pre-emptive, historical case-grounded audits of documentation, generating a "Contextual Density" score that identifies friction zones. The second engine is an autonomous Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) agent that surfaces in-situ via a location-intelligent assistant window, resolving queries in real-time. By functioning as a strategic "defensive barrier" at the point of origin, SENTINEL demonstrates how a proactive AI assistant can drive high-fidelity, in-situ case deflection. items.title: Shaping Europe’s digital future
items.summary: EU KIDS Act to restrict social media platforms' access to children in the EU The European Commission has adopted the EU KIDS Act to enhance the online safety of children throughout the Union. The proposal prohibits social media platforms from accessing children under the age of 13 and sets an EU-wide minimum age for minors to open an account of their own at the age of 15, thereby ensuring a gradual approach. The KIDS Act also reverses the burden of proof. Now, service providers will have to show that their services are age-appropriate and safe by design . items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. This year, the administration advanced reforms targeting childhood health, food quality, and preventive care while increasing transparency and accountability in healthcare systems. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. By prioritizing prevention over treatment and empowering families with better information and choices, the administration is addressing the root causes of poor health outcomes. These efforts are improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and ensuring a healthier future for the next generation of Americans. items.content: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program. Three grand challenges Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time. Efficiency . Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere. Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029 . Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions. PODCAST SERIES AI Testing and Evaluation: Learnings from Science and Industry Discover how Microsoft is learning from other domains to advance evaluation and testing as a pillar of AI governance. Listen now Opens in a new tab More than a decade of work For more than a decade, Microsoft Research has worked on making zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing practical. Early research followed two approaches, both practical only for small programs. The first (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) lets a verifier check a long computation through a short conversation with the prover using a technique called the sum-check protocol (opens in new tab) , but this applied only to computations with a particular layered structure. The second (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) used elliptic-curve cryptography to create very small proofs for almost any computation. But this requires a one-time trusted setup involving secret information which, if leaked, could allow anyone to forge proofs. This approach is also vulnerable to quantum computers. In 2019, a new zero-knowledge proof system called Spartan returned to the sum-check approach and made it work for general-purpose programs without a trusted setup. Spartan can also be instantiated with different cryptographic building blocks. That flexibility is what later allowed the proof system to be built on hash functions alone. A sequence of results then filled in the remaining pieces: Phalanx (opens in new tab) , in 2021, showed how to exploit repetition, such as a processor running the same instruction cycle on every step, to prove computations an order of magnitude faster than Spartan. Magnetar’s processor description is built on this idea. Nova (opens in new tab) , HyperNova (opens in new tab) , NeutronNova (opens in new tab) , Neo and SuperNeo (opens in new tab) showed that stopping Spartan’s proving early, and folding the partial results together, makes it practical to prove computations of any size at far lower cost. Brakedown (opens in new tab) , in 2021, introduced a fast hash-based commitment scheme and combined it with Spartan, giving the first Spartan variant whose security rests on standard hash functions. Spice (opens in new tab) , Lasso (opens in new tab) , Nebula (opens in new tab) , and then Twist and Shout (opens in new tab) made the memory operations at the heart of a general-purpose processor inexpensive to prove, and Jolt (opens in new tab) showed that combining them with Spartan can efficiently prove the execution of a complete processor. Earlier this year, Vega (opens in new tab) applied this line of work to digital identity, proving facts from a government credential in under a tenth of a second . More recently, BinarySpartan (opens in new tab) brought Spartan to binary fields, where a processor’s logic and standard hash functions can be efficiently expressed. BinarySpartan also relies on Ligerito (opens in new tab) , a Brakedown-style commitment scheme with much shorter proofs, and on ring switching (opens in new tab) , which makes it efficient to commit to vectors of bits. Each of these solved a piece of the problem. Magnetar is where the pieces come together. Magnetar Magnetar is a zero-knowledge virtual machine, or zkVM, and it makes major progress on all three challenges at once. Figure 1. Magnetar proves a program’s execution and returns a small proof that anyone can check, with security resting only on standard hash functions. It is general-purpose. Magnetar proves the execution of RISC-V, an open processor architecture with mature compilers for every mainstream language. A developer writes a program in Rust, Go, or C, compiles it as usual, and Magnetar proves it as written. Consider what this means in practice. A business policy, a data pipeline, or an interpreter for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is just a program, and the engineers who already maintain it can prove their executions exactly as written. As a result, proving stops being a specialist activity. It is faster than prior systems in the same class. Magnetar proves 7.2 to 8.7 million processor instructions per second on a laptop. Across 15 benchmark programs, from cryptographic hashing to token transfers inside a small EVM interpreter, it is 10 to 39 times faster on average than the fastest existing zkVMs on the same machine, and more than 300 times faster than two others on a token-transfer benchmark. An optimized Magnetar proves 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each speedup reported here by about 1.3×. Its proofs verify in about 12 milliseconds. Its security rests on standard cryptography. Magnetar depends on a standard hash function such as SHA-256 or SHA-3, the same primitives that already protect every organization’s systems. It requires no elliptic curves, no lattices, no special-purpose hash functions, no trusted setup, and no unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes. Hash functions are the most thoroughly studied primitives in the cryptographic toolkit, and they are the basis of the stateless hash-based signatures that NIST standardized as its own conservative post-quantum option. For a system that must still be trustworthy in many decades to come, relying only on standard hash functions removes a cryptographic migration from the roadmap. The same design decision pays a second dividend. Checking a Magnetar proof consists mostly of evaluating standard hash functions and binary-field arithmetic, which are exactly the operations Magnetar proves efficiently. Verifying a proof is therefore an ordinary workload for it. This is what allows Magnetar to prove computations of any size, by proving them in pieces and then combining the pieces. This also allows Magnetar to prove a long-running system such as a ledger or a blockchain. The technical paper gives the full design, security analysis, and measurements. Looking ahead Magnetar advances zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing to a stage where they can be built on the cryptography that organizations already trust, at speeds that make it usable, by engineers who write normal code. Magnetar enables a future where cryptographic proofs are a routine output of computation. We expect that technology leaders will stop asking whether proofs of execution are practical and focus instead on which results would they prefer to verify rather than taking on trust . If you’re interested in exploring how zero-knowledge proofs can support your use case, we’d love to hear from you (opens in new tab) . items.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. Spotlight: Event Series Microsoft Research Forum Join us for a continuous exchange of ideas about research in the era of general AI. Watch the latest episodes on demand. Watch on-demand Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project. items.content: At a glance Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings. The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss. Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material. Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform , which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars: Synthetic enterprise environments : simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data Automated query generation pipelines for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets Structured quality frameworks to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation Figure 1: Components of Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data ? In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. Synthetic enterprise environments Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve. Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments : simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful. Grounding in real world signals To ensure our synthetic environments are realistic, we grounded them in publicly available real world data sources. O*NET data from the U.S. Department of Labor’s occupational database was used to make synthetic employee roles and responsibilities realistic, calibrate the mix and frequency of work activities assigned to different roles, and tailor industry specific workflows such as clinical trial reviews or portfolio updates. Online job postings provide realistic role titles, reporting hierarchies, and departmental compositions. SEC filings inform organizational scale, business unit structures, and financial contexts. All of these sources are publicly available and have been reviewed and approved by Microsoft’s legal and policy organization. Figure 2: Real signals from public datasets that are used to ground the evaluation data generation Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure. Industry specific simulation We generated three synthetic environments across multiple industries, each with distinct characteristics that mirror real world usage: A pharmaceutical environment that includes regulatory submission workflows, clinical trial discussions, and cross functional safety review meetings A capital markets environment featuring deal pipelines, compliance communications, and client portfolio reviews An IT/software company that simulates sprint planning, code review discussions, and product launch coordination Figure 3: Industries targeted for industry evaluation data generation This industry specificity ensures that our evaluation queries test Copilot against the kinds of questions real users in those domains actually ask, rather than relying on generic test cases that may not surface domain specific failure modes. Automated query generation While synthetic environments provide the substrate for evaluation, they face a key limitation: we still need realistic evaluation queries. These are the questions that test whether Copilot can surface the right information, synthesize it correctly, and present it helpfully. Manually writing thousands of grounded, industry specific queries is prohibitively expensive and slow. That’s where our automated pipeline comes in. The six-stage pipeline Figure 4: Query customization pipeline that turns generic query templates into realistic, industry-specific queries We built an automated pipeline that turns simple, generic query ideas into realistic, industry-specific questions for Copilot. It starts with a large library of common workplace tasks, narrows them down to what’s relevant for a given industry, and adapts them using domain-specific language and context. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios. Validating synthetic quality Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions: Structural fidelity : Does the organizational structure reflect realistic reporting hierarchies, team sizes, and cross functional relationships? Contextual relevance : Are the queries and workflows representative of actual enterprise usage patterns? Behavioral realism : Do the simulated users exhibit human-like communication patterns and collaboration dynamics? Content safety : Is the generated content free of harmful, offensive, or personally identifiable material, and does it avoid impersonating real individuals? End-to-end automation While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including: Reproducibility : Manual processes produce subtly different results each time, making it difficult to compare evaluations across releases. Scale : The number of industry verticals and configuration variants exceeds what any team can reasonably produce by hand. Iteration speed : Manual creation takes days, delaying essential feedback and slowing down development cycles. Cross-team consistency : Without standardized tooling, different teams produce evaluation datasets with incompatible formats and quality levels. This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results. video series On Second Thought A video series with Sinead Bovell built around the questions everyone’s asking about AI. With expert voices from across Microsoft, we break down the tension and promise of this rapidly changing technology, exploring what’s evolving and what’s possible. Explore the series Opens in a new tab Privacy and safety by design Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline . Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or Responsible AI risk. Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline. This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible. Results and impact Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions. On synthetic data quality , our internal scoring system showed significant quality gains in the structural, contextual, and statistical fidelity of the generated data. Across our composite quality metric (which measures how closely synthetic data mirrors the complexity and patterns of real enterprise environments), scores improved 39% compared to our initial generation approach. Some industry-specific environments reached quality scores above 0.9 out of 1.0, demonstrating that domain focused generation produces highly realistic evaluation environments. The improvements were obtained in part by incorporating realistic, industry signals and in part by automating quality improvements via key composite quality metrics that help improve the structural integrity, contextual coherence and statistical diversity of our synthetic industry environments. On scale and efficiency , each synthetic environment now contains hundreds of users with complete communication histories across three industry verticals. Evaluation dataset creation has gone from multi-day manual effort to automated pipeline runs. On organizational adoption , our industry evaluation data generation platforms have been published to an internal shared catalog for cross-team reuse and established as the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. The difference wasn’t just incremental. It was a shift in how teams approach evaluation: from ad hoc, manual processes to standardized, reproducible infrastructure. Conclusion As we continue to expand what Microsoft Copilot can do, from single turn Q&A to agentic multi-step workflows, our commitment to evaluation remains at the heart of our approach. In enterprise AI, quality isn’t just about accuracy or speed. It’s about trust. Organizations need confidence that AI systems handle their information correctly, and that confidence can only come from thorough, repeatable evaluation. That trust rests on two commitments woven through everything we build: rigorous privacy protection and proactive content safety. Looking ahead, Microsoft Copilot is tackling even more exciting evaluation challenges: How do we assess the quality of multi-turn agentic interactions? How do we extend synthetic environments to capture organizational dynamics evolving over months or years? How do we build evaluation frameworks for AI systems that take actions, not just generate text? These are the kinds of questions our team is working on next. At Microsoft, we’re not just building AI. We’re building the infrastructure to ensure it works reliably for every enterprise, in every industry, at every scale . Thanks to everyone who’s worked on Industry Evaluation Datasets ! Validating synthetic quality Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions: Structural fidelity : Does the organizational structure reflect realistic reporting hierarchies, team sizes, and cross functional relationships? Contextual relevance : Are the queries and workflows representative of actual enterprise usage patterns? Behavioral realism : Do the simulated users exhibit human-like communication patterns and collaboration dynamics? Content safety : Is the generated content free of harmful, offensive, or personally identifiable material, and does it avoid impersonating real individuals? End-to-end automation While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including: Reproducibility : Manual processes produce subtly different results each time, making it difficult to compare evaluations across releases. Scale : The number of industry verticals and configuration variants exceeds what any team can reasonably produce by hand. Iteration speed : Manual creation takes days, delaying essential feedback and slowing down development cycles. Cross-team consistency : Without standardized tooling, different teams produce evaluation datasets with incompatible formats and quality levels. This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results. video series On Second Thought A video series with Sinead Bovell built around the questions everyone’s asking about AI. With expert voices from across Microsoft, we break down the tension and promise of this rapidly changing technology, exploring what’s evolving and what’s possible. Explore the series Opens in a new tab Privacy and safety by design Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline . Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or Responsible AI risk. Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline. This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible. Results and impact Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions. On synthetic data quality , our internal scoring system showed significant quality gains in the structural, contextual, and statistical fidelity of the generated data. Across our composite quality metric (which measures how closely synthetic data mirrors the complexity and patterns of real enterprise environments), scores improved 39% compared to our initial generation approach. Some industry-specific environments reached quality scores above 0.9 out of 1.0, demonstrating that domain focused generation produces highly realistic evaluation environments. The improvements were obtained in part by incorporating realistic, industry signals and in part by automating quality improvements via key composite quality metrics that help improve the structural integrity, contextual coherence and statistical diversity of our synthetic industry environments. On scale and efficiency , each synthetic environment now contains hundreds of users with complete communication histories across three industry verticals. Evaluation dataset creation has gone from multi-day manual effort to automated pipeline runs. On organizational adoption , our industry evaluation data generation platforms have been published to an internal shared catalog for cross-team reuse and established as the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. The difference wasn’t just incremental. It was a shift in how teams approach evaluation: from ad hoc, manual processes to standardized, reproducible infrastructure. Conclusion As we continue to expand what Microsoft Copilot can do, from single turn Q&A to agentic multi-step workflows, our commitment to evaluation remains at the heart of our approach. In enterprise AI, quality isn’t just about accuracy or speed. It’s about trust. Organizations need confidence that AI systems handle their information correctly, and that confidence can only come from thorough, repeatable evaluation. That trust rests on two commitments woven through everything we build: rigorous privacy protection and proactive content safety. Looking ahead, Microsoft Copilot is tackling even more exciting evaluation challenges: How do we assess the quality of multi-turn agentic interactions? How do we extend synthetic environments to capture organizational dynamics evolving over months or years? How do we build evaluation frameworks for AI systems that take actions, not just generate text? These are the kinds of questions our team is working on next. At Microsoft, we’re not just building AI. We’re building the infrastructure to ensure it works reliably for every enterprise, in every industry, at every scale . Thanks to everyone who’s worked on Industry Evaluation Datasets !
