items.content: Back to Articles Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms Published October 29, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 19 +13 Mattt mattt Follow Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do. Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive. In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap , we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model. Today we're announcing two packages: AnySpeechRecognizer implements Apple's new speech-to-text API with a choice of recognition engine, including NVIDIA's Parakeet and Alibaba's Qwen3-ASR running locally on Core ML, and adds speaker diarization to track who speaks when. AnyDecisionModel answers yes-or-no, multiple-choice, and rating-scale questions with typed results and probabilities. It derives each answer from the model's probabilities instead of generating text, using a model on your device with MLX, Core AI, or llama.cpp, or a decision model from Jev or Ollama. Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device. AnySpeechRecognizer Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer , Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen. It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine: - import Speech + import AnySpeechRecognizer The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer , SpeechTranscriber , DictationTranscriber , SpeechDetector , and AssetInventory , with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber: let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber ( model: ParakeetSpeechModel (variant: .v3), transcriptionOptions: [], reportingOptions: [.volatileResults], attributeOptions: [.audioTimeRange] ) The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework. Meet the models Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 . It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale. Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3 . It was more accurate in most of our measurements. Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet . All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence. Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one: let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber ( model: QwenSpeechModel (variant: .large, language: Locale . Language (identifier: "yue" )), transcriptionOptions: [], reportingOptions: [], attributeOptions: [] ) Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input. To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started. Core ML models on the Hub To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub: Model Core ML conversion Original checkpoint License Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 mattt/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3-coreml nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3 CC BY 4.0 Parakeet Ultra mattt/parakeet-ultra-coreml moondream/parakeet-ultra CC BY 4.0 Parakeet Unified EN 0.6B mattt/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b-coreml nvidia/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b NVIDIA Open Model License Qwen3-ASR 0.6B mattt/qwen3-asr-0.6b-coreml Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B-hf Apache 2.0 Qwen3-ASR 1.7B mattt/qwen3-asr-1.7b-coreml Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B-hf Apache 2.0 Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2 mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2-coreml nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2 CC BY 4.0 Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2.1 mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2.1-coreml nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1 NVIDIA Open Model License Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model. Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools. Speaker diarization When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline: let diarizer = SpeakerDiarizer (model: SortformerDiarizationModel ()) if let request = try await AssetInventory .assetInstallationRequest( supporting: [transcriber, diarizer] ) { try await request.downloadAndInstall() } let analyzer = SpeechAnalyzer (modules: [transcriber, diarizer]) The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today. The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1 , which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too. How well does it work? We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes: Transcriber test-clean test-other Parakeet v3, file 1.55% 2.78% Parakeet v3, live 4.73% 4.29% Parakeet Ultra, file 1.66% 2.55% Parakeet Ultra, live 2.65% 3.28% Parakeet Unified, file 1.43% 2.19% Parakeet Unified, live 1.45% 2.42% Apple's transcriber, file 2.12% 3.97% Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%. These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements . So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone. Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27. AnyDecisionModel AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly. It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification. What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them. Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives. Here's what a decision looks like in Swift: import AnyDecisionModel enum Department : String , Choosable { case billing, technical, sales } let ticket = "I was charged twice for my order, and now the app logs me out when I try to ask for a refund." let model = MLXDecisionModel (modelID: "mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit" ) let session = DecisionSession (model: model, state: .text(ticket)) let urgent = try await session.probability(of: "Does this convey urgency?" ) let team = try await session.choice( "Which team?" , from: Department . self ) let anger = try await session.score( "How frustrated?" , levels: [ "Calm" , "Frustrated" , "Very angry" ] ) urgent is a Double . team is a Choice<Department> containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable , team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch . If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch. For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass. Try it out: Emoji Magnet Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back. The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example: Statement: a heavy winter coat fits the description "things you wear". Is this statement true? The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY , the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive. Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository. Decision heads and Clef Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant. AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX: let model = MLXHeadDecisionModel ( modelID: "mlx-community/clef-flash-4bit" , head: .jointSchema ) You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states. Calibrating and checking probabilities Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration , which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results. Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation. Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere. Backends AnyDecisionModel has six backends: MLX runs a small language model on Apple silicon with mlx-swift-lm and downloads it from the Hub. MLX decision heads run a model with its own trained decision head, such as Clef. Core AI does the same as MLX with a Core AI model on macOS 27 and iOS 27. llama.cpp reads decisions from a local GGUF model through llama.swift . Jev calls TypeSafe's Jev through the System One API , or any server that implements it, such as Kev . Ollama calls a System One decision model on a local Ollama server or in Ollama's cloud. It requires Ollama 0.35.0 or later, or 0.40.5 or later for cloud models. The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit. Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX , CoreAI , or Llama trait for the local backends. Get started Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime. Add the packages to your Package.swift : dependencies: [ .package(url: "https://github.com/mattt/AnySpeechRecognizer" , from: "0.1.0" ), .package( url: "https://github.com/mattt/AnyDecisionModel" , from: "0.6.0" , traits: [ "MLX" ] ), ] For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x. Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear , that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple , --backend parakeet , or --backend qwen ; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets. Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories. Links AnySpeechRecognizer on GitHub AnyDecisionModel on GitHub AnyDecisionModel-Examples on GitHub AnyLanguageModel on GitHub swift-huggingface on GitHub Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow. Language (identifier: "yue" )), transcriptionOptions: [], reportingOptions: [], attributeOptions: [] ) Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input. To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model. Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%. These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements . So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone. Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27. AnyDecisionModel AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly. It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification. What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them. Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives. Here's what a decision looks like in Swift: import AnyDecisionModel enum Department : String , Choosable { case billing, technical, sales } let ticket = "I was charged twice for my order, and now the app logs me out when I try to ask for a refund." let model = MLXDecisionModel (modelID: "mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit" ) let session = DecisionSession (model: model, state: .text(ticket)) let urgent = try await session.probability(of: "Does this convey urgency?" ) let team = try await session.choice( "Which team?" , from: Department . self ) let anger = try await session.score( "How frustrated?" , levels: [ "Calm" , "Frustrated" , "Very angry" ] ) urgent is a Double . team is a Choice<Department> containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable , team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch . If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch. For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example: Statement: a heavy winter coat fits the description "things you wear". Is this statement true? The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive. Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository. Decision heads and Clef Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere. MLX decision heads run a model with its own trained decision head, such as Clef. Core AI does the same as MLX with a Core AI model on macOS 27 and iOS 27. llama.cpp reads decisions from a local GGUF model through llama.swift . Jev calls TypeSafe's Jev through the System One API , or any server that implements it, such as Kev . Ollama calls a System One decision model on a local Ollama server or in Ollama's cloud. It requires Ollama 0.35.0 or later, or 0.40.5 or later for cloud models. The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime. Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. items.content: Back to Articles StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents Enterprise Article Published November 3, 2026 Upvote 18 +12 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 📄 Tech Report | 🤗 Data | 💻 Code We’re introducing StateBench , a benchmark for long-context state tracking —how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve. State tracking underlies tasks from reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, to following a story as characters physically move around and objects change hands. For example, if a mystery novel states that “John gave Mary the knife” right before a murder occurs, it’s important to know that the state of each character has changed. However, not all state-tracking problems are created equal: some require only finding the latest update; harder ones require following a chain of changes, where one missed step can throw off the final answer. For example, a harder variant of our mystery state tracking would be if John gave Mary the item in his backpack, with it previously known that Edward put a knife in John’s backpack. Transformers have well-documented theoretical limits on hard variants of state tracking with long dependency chains, helping motivate recurrent and hybrid architectures such as Gated DeltaNet that carry a running memory forward. Existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, but as these designs become more common, researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle. We would like to understand the differences between architectures not just on the hardest kinds of state tracking, but also on the simpler, potentially more common kinds. To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer. Four levels of state tracking StateBench consists of four difficulty levels that permit increasingly complex state update operations. For programmers, these levels of state tracking complexity can be understood as allowing different types of variable assignment operations: R-trivial problems use immutable assignment. A variable’s value never changes, so the model only needs to recover what it was first set to. In code, this looks like let x = 4; in everyday life, it’s like a birth date—it stays fixed. Aperiodic problems allow reassignment by value. The model needs to find the most recent value and can ignore earlier ones. In code, this looks like x = 4 followed later by x = 2; in everyday life, it’s like a thermostat, where the latest setting determines the current temperature. Soluble problems add self-referential updates. Each update builds on the current value, so the model has to carry changes forward rather than simply find the latest assignment. In code, this looks like x = x + 5; in everyday life, it’s like a game score, where each point adds to the running total. General finite problems add assignment by reference. One variable can take on another variable’s current value, creating dependencies across updates. In code, this looks like x = y or swapping two variables. Imagine a magician hiding a ball under one of five cups, then repeatedly swapping their positions. Finding the ball means keeping track of how those swaps change its location. This illustrates the S₅ state-tracking problem: following how successive swaps rearrange five objects. It belongs to the hardest of our four levels and is discussed in previous work on the limits of state tracking . These levels can be intuitively understood in terms of variable assignments, but they also represent theoretically motivated distinctions in state tracking rooted in Krohn–Rhodes theory, a branch of algebra that describes how state-tracking problems – which can be viewed as word problems over finite monoids – can be decomposed into atomic primitives. Each level in our hierarchy corresponds to a class of state-tracking problems that can be built out of a different set of primitives. To compare the four levels fairly, we start with a general finite sequence of variable assignments and derive three easier versions from it, producing four comparable StateBench problems—one at each difficulty level. All four use the same number of variables and distinct values, with assignments appearing at the same points in the sequence; only the type of assignment changes. What we found Pretrained models We tested a range of open pretrained models on the r-trivial, aperiodic, and general finite levels of StateBench to see where their state tracking breaks down, and whether different architectures fail where theory predicts. Under standard theoretical assumptions, transformers can handle r-trivial robustly (and soluble and aperiodic to some degree) but are predicted to fail on general problems. In contrast, Gated DeltaNet with a more flexible memory update can, in principle, handle all four levels. We started with open pretrained models, where the training data and context lengths are fully documented. These included two 7-billion-parameter models, Olmo 3 (a transformer) and Olmo Hybrid (which adds Gated DeltaNet layers), along with smaller models with 275 million and 2.7 billion parameters. All of these models were pretrained on the same data; none had seen contexts longer than 64,000 tokens during training, and we tested most of them on inputs well beyond that length. When we scored each model, almost all performed well on r-trivial problems, lost accuracy on aperiodic ones as inputs grew, and stayed at chance on general finite problems. Problem format mattered here—the 275-million-parameter hybrid and Gated DeltaNet models scored near the ceiling on RULER-style r-trivial problems but were near chance on the same problems framed as spreadsheet edits. That gap is one reason StateBench tests the same underlying problem in several formats. Frontier models We then tested four frontier models – Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna – asking them to read each sequence of variable assignments and generate the final value of every variable. All four performed well on r-trivial and aperiodic problems. But on soluble and general finite problems, accuracy fell sharply as inputs grew longer, dropping to 13% or lower on the longest general finite problems. One likely factor is sensitivity ; at these harder levels, many more steps can affect the final answer, leaving less room for a model to miss an update without getting the result wrong. Models trained directly on the task Next, we investigated whether models’ difficulty with the harder levels reflects limits of the architectures themselves, or whether pretraining simply doesn’t teach models to solve them. Targeted direct training is a more favorable setting that reveals to what degree state-tracking issues come from the underlying architecture and optimizer rather than the data used to pretrain a model. We trained several 275-million-parameter models from scratch on StateBench: two transformer variants, two hybrids, and two Gated DeltaNet variants with different memory-update constraints. The models trained on sequences of up to 256 assignments and were tested on sequences as long as 64,000 assignments, or 250 times the maximum training length. The architectures began to diverge as sequences grew longer. Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models generalized almost perfectly on r-trivial, aperiodic, and soluble problems out to the longest sequences we tested, tens of thousands of assignments. Transformers learned the easier levels but degraded on longer sequences, and they never learned general finite problems. On the hardest level, the Gated DeltaNet variant with a more flexible memory update generalized the farthest, staying near perfect out to roughly 10 times the length of the longest sequences it saw during training. For Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models, the gap points to training rather than architecture; trained directly, they learned to handle state-tracking levels their pretrained counterparts couldn’t. Transformers were different—even trained directly, they could never learn the hardest level. Open questions and the release Some questions remain open. Our new proof shows that Gated DeltaNet with a more limited memory update (non-negative eigenvalues) can solve all aperiodic tasks and certain periodic tasks, such as tracking whether a repeated input has occurred an even or odd number of times, under the paper’s fixed-precision arithmetic with rounding. Its exact placement in the hierarchy remains open, including whether it can solve all soluble tasks and how numerical precision or combining it with attention layers affects its capabilities. StateBench also assumes a fixed number of variables, while real tasks often introduce new entities over time. In a long conversation, for example, new people and objects can appear as it unfolds, and the model has to begin tracking them too. The current framework doesn’t yet cover that setting. As new flavors of recurrent and hybrid architectures emerge, understanding which kinds of state tracking each can handle could help guide how future systems are developed and trained. We hope StateBench gives researchers a finer-grained way to find where models break down—and to build training and evaluation data for the capabilities that still fall short. More fundamentally, we hope it serves as a North Star for researchers to develop new architectures with more robust state-tracking abilities compared to current models. items.content: Back to Articles Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language Enterprise Article Published November 3, 2026 Upvote 11 +5 Praveen Venkateswaran praveenv Follow ibm-research Anupama Murthi anupamamurthi Follow ibm-research Hamid Adebayo harmedox Follow ibm-research Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all. Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other. Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language , and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it. Why decks are hard for small models A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at. It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from. It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent. There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them. Build it like a human: a designer and a coder Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter: The designer reads the plan and writes a structured JSON brief: the palette, the type system, and for each slide its layout, its exact content and a short design rationale. The coder takes one slide's spec from the brief and writes the pptxgenjs JavaScript that draws it, preceded by its reasoning. Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster. We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×. Synthesizing decks and their reasoning There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides. Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example: "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance." The coder reasons about geometry: "The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart." The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example. The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest. What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions. Steering a deck in plain English Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives , short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]] : ## Rollout plan - March: pilot with two teams - May: security review complete - July: rollout to all of engineering - September: company-wide launch - November: first adoption review [[make this a timeline]] The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead. The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase. Category Example directive Layout [[make this a timeline]] Tone [[be candid, no spin]] Audience [[this is for the board]] Order [[lead with the ask]] Leaving out [[no pricing]] Emphasis [[highlight the headline number]] Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive. Building a check-and-repair harness Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first. Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned. First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code. The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse. Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right). To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average. Evaluation We evaluate on PresentBench , which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper. Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean. Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model. PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close. What's next The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training. We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling ) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining. What we learned Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts: Put the reasoning in the data. Training on why a choice was made, including what was rejected, teaches more than the choice alone. Fix the examples before adding a rule. When the teacher got something wrong, our first instinct was to add a rule to its prompt, and that rarely helped. The teacher copied its reference decks far more than it followed instructions, so fixing the reference was what actually changed its output. Make repairs safe by default. A fix that's kept only when it measurably helps can run on every output. Build the checker first. It's what makes the data trustworthy and the outputs safe to ship. items.content: Back to Articles Transformers Model Integration Contracts Published November 3, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 13 +7 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months. When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it. Why bugs reach main Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels. The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main. Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study , the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB. This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU. Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine. Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main. Introducing Model Integration Contracts transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts: a fixture : the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned a usage path : a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the model, such as generating text or running a training step baselines : the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a human The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines. A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic . For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt: inputs = tokenizer( "The capital of France is" , return_tensors= "pt" ) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 4 , do_sample= False ) new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:] print (tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens= True )) It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md . A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later. On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes. The UMT5 regression We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28 . Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20. One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint. We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup. The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details. How models are shrunk The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear. The recipe now has four steps: Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds, including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers. Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible. We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the ModelTester in test_modeling_<model>.py already picks a small config by hand, so we take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name. Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte. Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test. Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds. Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR. We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail. The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style. Building MICs with agents Our CLI, tmic , creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review. To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model : pip install "transformers-mic[runtime]" "hf-doc-builder @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/doc-builder.git" hf auth login tmic run org/model --local-only --fixtures-only --no-history --bill-to '' It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account ( --bill-to '' ). The CLI docs cover the individual steps. We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space . Random vs Overfit With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path. So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study , the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24. That gives us two ways to build the weights: Start with random weights and a fixed seed. Overfit on a few examples, like "The capital of France is" => "Paris". The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed. So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both. Open questions As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet: How many real bugs does it catch on PRs, not just in replays? How often does it send us chasing false alarms? How much work do baseline reviews take? We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss. Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for. Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs. items.raw_text: Back to Articles Transformers Model Integration Contracts Published November 3, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 13 +7 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months. When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it. Why bugs reach main Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels. The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main. Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study , the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB. This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU. Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine. Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main. Introducing Model Integration Contracts transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts: a fixture : the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned a usage path : a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the model, such as generating text or running a training step baselines : the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a human The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines. A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic . For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt: inputs = tokenizer( "The capital of France is" , return_tensors= "pt" ) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 4 , do_sample= False ) new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:] print (tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens= True )) It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md . A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later. On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes. The UMT5 regression We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28 . Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20. One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint. We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup. The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details. How models are shrunk The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear. The recipe now has four steps: Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds, including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers. Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible. We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the ModelTester in test_modeling_<model>.py already picks a small config by hand, so we take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name. Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte. Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test. Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds. Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR. We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail. The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style. Building MICs with agents Our CLI, tmic , creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account ( --bill-to '' ). The CLI docs cover the individual steps. We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. items.summary: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.05373 (cs) [Submitted on 3 Nov 2026] Title: Aligning Language Models with General Preferences: An Empirical Study of Direct Nash Optimization Authors: Austin Tsai , Saurav Nanda , Ganapathy Parthasarathy , Bhuvnesh Kumar , Parivesh Choudhary View a PDF of the paper titled Aligning Language Models with General Preferences: An Empirical Study of Direct Nash Optimization, by Austin Tsai and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Direct Nash Optimization (DNO) aligns a language model to a general preference function by approximating the Nash equilibrium of a two-player preference game. Its practical variant, DNO-Prct, iterates on-policy sampling, LLM-based rating of the samples together with a teacher's gold response, large-margin preference-pair selection and a DPO-style contrastive update. We re-implement DNO-Prct independently and study it on two open-weight instruct models, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1
items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.05373 (cs) [Submitted on 3 Nov 2026] Title: Aligning Language Models with General Preferences: An Empirical Study of Direct Nash Optimization Authors: Austin Tsai , Saurav Nanda , Ganapathy Parthasarathy , Bhuvnesh Kumar , Parivesh Choudhary View a PDF of the paper titled Aligning Language Models with General Preferences: An Empirical Study of Direct Nash Optimization, by Austin Tsai and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Direct Nash Optimization (DNO) aligns a language model to a general preference function by approximating the Nash equilibrium of a two-player preference game. Its practical variant, DNO-Prct, iterates on-policy sampling, LLM-based rating of the samples together with a teacher's gold response, large-margin preference-pair selection and a DPO-style contrastive update. We re-implement DNO-Prct independently and study it on two open-weight instruct models, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1, with GPT-4o or a larger open-weight model of the same family as the annotator. On AlpacaEval 2.0 with GPT-4o as judge, three iterations raise the length-controlled (LC) win rate against GPT-4o from 31.7% to 45.3% for Llama and from 6.8% to 18.4% for Mistral, and the tuned 8B model scores above Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on every reported win rate. With same-family open-weight annotators, the runs retain 62% (Llama) and 82% (Mistral) of the LC gain achieved with GPT-4o as annotator, so the rating step does not require a proprietary model. In a separate ablation configuration, variants that remove the gold responses, remove the data look-back, or accept only teacher-preferred pairs score 6 to 10 LC points below the full procedure, whereas varying the number of on-policy samples per prompt (1 to 7) moves the LC win rate by at most 2.1 points, and a margin sweep (1 to 5) run in its own pipeline by at most 2.4 points. We also report the cost of the pipeline and where the practical algorithm departs from the theory it approximates. All results are single runs, and GPT-4o is both the teacher and the evaluation judge; we discuss what this implies for the reported gains. Comments: 19 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. In a separate ablation configuration, variants that remove the gold responses, remove the data look-back, or accept only teacher-preferred pairs score 6 to 10 LC points below the full procedure, whereas varying the number of on-policy samples per prompt (1 to 7) moves the LC win rate by at most 2.1 points, and a margin sweep (1 to 5) run in its own pipeline by at most 2.4 points. We also report the cost of the pipeline and where the practical algorithm departs from the theory it approximates. All results are single runs, and GPT-4o is both the teacher and the evaluation judge; we discuss what this implies for the reported gains. Comments: 19 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. items.content: Aligning Language Models with General Preferences: An Empirical Study of Direct Nash Optimization Austin Tsai Affiliation: Synopsys, Inc., Sunnyvale, CA, USA Saurav Nanda Affiliation: Synopsys, Inc., Sunnyvale, CA, USA Ganapathy Parthasarathy Affiliation: Synopsys, Inc., Sunnyvale, CA, USA Bhuvnesh Kumar Affiliation: Synopsys, Inc., Sunnyvale, CA, USA Correspondence to: bhuvnesh@synopsys.com Parivesh Choudhary Affiliation: Synopsys, Inc., Sunnyvale, CA, USA Abstract Direct Nash Optimization (DNO) aligns a language model to a general preference function by approximating the Nash equilibrium of a two-player preference game. Its practical variant, DNO-Prct, iterates on-policy sampling, LLM-based rating of the samples together with a teacher’s gold response, large-margin preference-pair selection and a DPO-style contrastive update. We re-implement DNO-Prct independently and study it on two open-weight instruct models, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1, with GPT-4o or a larger open-weight model of the same family as the annotator. On AlpacaEval 2.0 with GPT-4o as judge, three iterations raise the length-controlled (LC) win rate against GPT-4o from 31.7% to 45.3% for Llama and from 6.8% to 18.4% for Mistral, and the tuned 8B model scores above Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on every reported win rate. With same-family open-weight annotators, the runs retain 62% (Llama) and 82% (Mistral) of the LC gain achieved with GPT-4o as annotator, so the rating step does not require a proprietary model. In a separate ablation configuration, variants that remove the gold responses, remove the data look-back, or accept only teacher-preferred pairs score 6 to 10 LC points below the full procedure, whereas varying the number of on-policy samples per prompt (1 to 7) moves the LC win rate by at most 2.1 points, and a margin sweep (1 to 5) run in its own pipeline by at most 2.4 points. We also report the cost of the pipeline and where the practical algorithm departs from the theory it approximates. All results are single runs, and GPT-4o is both the teacher and the evaluation judge; we discuss what this implies for the reported gains. Keywords: RLHF, preference optimization, Direct Nash Optimization, DPO, LLM alignment, AlpacaEval, LLM-as-a-judge † † affiliationnotice: Work done while all authors were at Synopsys, Inc. 1 Introduction Pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly ( Radford et al., 2018 ; Radford et al., 2019 ; Brown et al., 2020 ; Rae et al., 2021 ) . Trained only to predict the next token, they are not by themselves aligned with what humans prefer. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) ( Christiano et al., 2017 ; Stiennon et al., 2020 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Bai et al., 2022 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; OpenAI, 2023 ) bridges this gap by collecting human preferences, training a reward model on them, and optimizing the policy with reinforcement learning. Single-stage contrastive methods such as Direct Preference Optimization ( Rafailov et al., 2023 , DPO;) remove the explicit reward model. In their standard formulations, both assume a pointwise (Bradley–Terry) reward and therefore cannot represent intransitive preferences, which Liu et al. (2025) show arise with high probability under a Luce-type preference model; they are also vulnerable to reward hacking ( Amodei et al., 2016 ) , and a reward model or preference dataset fixed in advance becomes stale as the policy distribution shifts during training ( Ross et al., 2011 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ; Azar et al., 2024 ; Munos et al., 2024 ) . To address these limitations, a line of work optimizes the general preference function directly by finding the Nash equilibrium of a two-player game, solving that game with single-player (self-play) algorithms that exploit the symmetry of the preference function ( Munos et al., 2024 ; Swamy et al., 2024 ) . For a preference function with 𝒫 ⁡ ( y ≻ y ′ ∣ x ) + 𝒫 ⁡ ( y ′ ≻ y ∣ x ) = 1 \mathcal{P}(y\succ y^{\prime}\mid x)+\mathcal{P}(y^{\prime}\succ y\mid x)=1 and 𝒫 ( π ≻ π ′ ) := 𝔼 x ∼ ρ , y ∼ π ( ⋅ ∣ x ) , y ′ ∼ π ′ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) [ 𝒫 ( y ≻ y ′ ∣ x ) ] \mathcal{P}(\pi\succ\pi^{\prime}):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho,\,y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x),\,y^{\prime}\sim\pi^{\prime}(\cdot\mid x)}[\mathcal{P}(y\succ y^{\prime}\mid x)] for a prompt distribution ρ \rho , a Nash equilibrium is a policy π ⋆ \pi^{\star} with 𝒫 ⁡ ( π ⋆ ≻ π ) ≥ 1 2 \mathcal{P}(\pi^{\star}\succ\pi)\geq\tfrac{1}{2} for every competing policy π \pi in the policy class Π \Pi ; this policy is the Minimax Winner of the game. Rosset et al. (2024) propose Direct Nash Optimization (DNO): a provable algorithm whose iterates converge to the Nash equilibrium on average, together with a practical variant, DNO-Prct, which in their largest run, on about ten times more prompts over six iterations, brought a 7B model to a 33% length-controlled AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate against GPT-4 Turbo, with GPT-4 Turbo as annotator and gold-response source. DNO-Prct bundles several design choices: batched on-policy sampling, a teacher’s gold response among the candidates, LLM-based rating against a rubric, a minimum rating margin, and a decaying look-back over earlier pairs. To our knowledge no independent re-implementation of DNO-Prct has been published: its published results, including its ablations, use one base model and a proprietary annotator, so it is not known whether its gains and design choices transfer to other base models and annotators. This paper is an empirical study of DNO-Prct. We re-implemented the algorithm from the description in Rosset et al. (2024) , ran it on two open-weight instruct models with GPT-4o and with same-family open-weight models as annotators, and examined its main design choices. Throughout, “DNO” refers to DNO-Prct unless stated otherwise. Our contributions are as follows. (1) An independent re-implementation with a procedural description: We give the pair-construction procedure as pseudo-code (Appendix C ), the rating prompt verbatim (Appendix A ) and the hyperparameters and implementation settings (Appendix B ). Together with Rosset et al. (2024) , this describes the pipeline in enough detail to re-implement it. (2) Gains on two model families: Over three iterations the student’s length-controlled (LC) AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate against GPT-4o rises from 31.71% to 45.32% for Llama 3.1 8B Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) and from 6.77% to 18.44% for Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1 ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) . Under the same protocol, the tuned 8B model scores above Llama 3.1 70B Instruct, which has nearly nine times as many parameters, on all four reported win rates, and the tuned 7B model narrows its gap to Mixtral 8x7B Instruct v0.1 ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) on all four, to between 0.2 and 12.8 points (Section 5.3 ). (3) Open-weight annotators: Replacing GPT-4o with Llama 3.1 70B Instruct or Mistral Large 2 as the annotator retains 62% (Llama) and 82% (Mistral) of the LC gain against the GPT-4o opponent; against GPT-4-0613 the Llama run retains 45% and the Mistral run matches the GPT-4o-annotated run, so the rating step does not require a proprietary model (Section 5.4 ). (4) Which components matter: In a separate ablation configuration, variants that remove the gold responses, remove the data look-back, or restrict pair selection to teacher-preferred pairs score 6 to 10 LC points below the full procedure against GPT-4o (9 to 19 points against GPT-4-0613), whereas the number of on-policy samples per prompt (1 to 7) moves the LC win rate against GPT-4o by at most 2.1 points, and a margin sweep (1 to 5) run in its own pipeline by at most 2.4 points (Section 6 ). We also document the cost of the pipeline (Section 7 ) and the places where DNO-Prct departs from the theory it approximates (Section 6.6 ). Rosset et al. (2024, Section 5.2) compared large-margin filtering, on-policy sampling and the SPIN and DNO-Restrictive pair rules in their own setting, and their Table 2 tracks teacher- and student-preferred pairs and the average teacher and student ratings across iterations. We extend these analyses beyond that setting, to two further base models and to open-weight annotators, add sweeps of the rating margin and the number of samples, and repeat their teacher–student analysis (Section 6.5 ). The experiments were run in 2024, and Section 3 relates them to work that appeared during or after them, notably on preference leakage between data generator and judge ( Li et al., 2026 ) and on the exploitability of AlpacaEval ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . 2 Preliminaries: Direct Nash Optimization There are two variants of Direct Nash Optimization: the theoretical DNO (Algorithm 1 ) and the practical DNO-Prct. Rosset et al. (2024) define the reward of a response at iteration t t as its expected win rate against the current policy’s own samples under the preference function 𝒫 \mathcal{P} : r t ( x , y ) := 𝔼 y ′ ∼ π t ( ⋅ ∣ x ) [ 𝒫 ( y ≻ y ′ ∣ x ) ] , r_{t}(x,y):=\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{t}(\cdot\mid x)}\big[\mathcal{P}(y\succ y^{\prime}\mid x)\big], (1) for prompts x ∈ 𝒳 x\in\mathcal{X} and responses y ∈ 𝒴 y\in\mathcal{Y} . DNO aligns the implicit reward used by DPO with this preference-based reward.
