Algorithm 1 Direct Nash Optimization (adapted from Rosset et al., 2024 ) 0: preference function 𝒫 \mathcal{P} , KL coefficient η \eta , iterations N N , prompt distribution ρ \rho 1: Initialize π 1 ← unif ⁡ ( 𝒴 ) \pi_{1}\leftarrow\mathrm{unif}(\mathcal{Y}) . 2: for t = 1 , … , N t=1,\ldots,N do 3: Compute r t ​ ( x , y ) r_{t}(x,y) by Eq. ( 1 ) for all ( x , y ) ∈ 𝒳 × 𝒴 (x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y} . 4: Obtain π t + 1 \pi_{t+1} by Eq. ( 5 ), where 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{t} is drawn as x ∼ ρ x\sim\rho , y 1 ∼ μ 1 , t ( ⋅ ∣ x ) y_{1}\sim\mu_{1,t}(\cdot\mid x) , y 2 ∼ μ 2 , t ( ⋅ ∣ x ) y_{2}\sim\mu_{2,t}(\cdot\mid x) with μ 1 , t , μ 2 , t \mu_{1,t},\mu_{2,t} off-policy or on-policy ( π t \pi_{t} ). 5: end for 6: return π ¯ = unif ( π 1 : N ) \bar{\pi}=\mathrm{unif}(\pi_{1:N}) Guarantees: Each exact iteration is one step of soft policy iteration, a no-regret update, so the uniform mixture π ¯ \bar{\pi} of the iterates converges to the Nash equilibrium of the two-player preference game, the Minimax Winner ( Kreweras, 1965 ; Simpson, 1969 ; Kramer, 1973 ; Fishburn, 1984 ) ; the mixture argument is due to Swamy et al. (2024) , and Munos et al. (2024) establish last-iterate convergence for the regularized game. Rosset et al. (2024) also establish two further properties (their Section 3.1 and Theorem 1). The exact soft-policy-iteration update improves monotonically, 𝒫 ( π t + 1 ⋆ ≻ π t ) ≥ 1 2 + η 𝔼 x ∼ ρ [ D KL ( π t + 1 ⋆ ∥ π t ) ] \mathcal{P}(\pi^{\star}_{t+1}\succ\pi_{t})\geq\tfrac{1}{2}+\eta\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{\star}_{t+1}\,\|\,\pi_{t})] , and their Theorem 1 bounds the expected squared total-variation distance between the learned π t + 1 \pi_{t+1} and π t + 1 ⋆ \pi^{\star}_{t+1} in terms of the sample size, the size of the policy class, a boundedness constant R max R_{\max} and a data-dependent concentrability coefficient, so the improvement carries over up to that error. These statements hold under the assumptions of the cited results (realizability of the soft-policy-iteration target in the policy class, and boundedness), and the bound is informative only when the concentrability coefficient is small; neither condition is guaranteed for a neural policy class. The improvement is against the previous iterate under 𝒫 \mathcal{P} and ρ \rho ; it is not a statement that benchmark scores rise at every iteration or that the student surpasses a fixed teacher. The practical procedure below, with finite samples, LLM ratings, margin filtering, look-back and a single selected checkpoint, approximates the exact update and does not inherit these guarantees. DNO-Prct: The main obstacle in practice is the expectation in Eq. ( 1 ). Rosset et al. (2024) therefore propose DNO-Prct, each iteration of which has three steps: 1. Batched on-policy sampling and rating: K K outputs per prompt are sampled from the current policy π t \pi_{t} and, together with a gold response y gold y^{\mathrm{gold}} from a stronger teacher model, are scored by an annotator; the scores serve as a proxy for the pairwise win-rate ranking under 𝒫 \mathcal{P} . 2. Preference pair construction: Only pairs whose scores differ by a sufficiently large margin are kept, with the intent that the target σ ⁡ ( Δ t ⋆ ) \sigma(\Delta^{\star}_{t}) , after a rescaling of r t r_{t} , be close to one so that Eq. ( 5 ) reduces approximately to the pure contrastive (DPO) loss (an approximation discussed in Section 6.6 ); a decaying fraction of pairs from earlier iterations is mixed in (data look-back, described in Section 5.1 of Rosset et al. (2024) rather than in their Algorithm 2). 3. Contrastive update: The policy is trained with the DPO objective on the constructed pairs, with π t \pi_{t} as the reference policy. DNO-Prct is thus an iterative, on-policy form of DPO with the same contrastive objective; the difference lies in how the preference pairs are constructed (Figure 1 in Section 4.2 ). We refer readers to Rosset et al. (2024) for the derivation. 3 Related Work RLHF and offline contrastive alignment: The reward-model-plus-RL recipe ( Christiano et al., 2017 ; Stiennon et al., 2020 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Bai et al., 2022 ) is a standard route to aligned chat models. Offline contrastive methods such as DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , IPO ( Azar et al., 2024 ) and SimPO ( Meng et al., 2024 ) fit the policy directly to a preference dataset; Zephyr ( Tunstall et al., 2023 ) popularized distilled supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on UltraChat followed by DPO on UltraFeedback ( Cui et al., 2024 ) . DPO and SimPO inherit the transitivity of a pointwise (Bradley–Terry) reward, which IPO avoids, and DPO in particular is known to exploit response length ( Park et al., 2024 ) . Meng et al. (2024) report that Llama-3-8B-Instruct trained with SimPO reaches 44.7% LC on the public AlpacaEval 2.0 leaderboard, above Llama-3-70B-Instruct (34.4%), so a small model scoring above a larger sibling on this metric is not by itself evidence of a better algorithm. Iterative, online and self-play alignment: Iterative DPO ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Xiong et al., 2024 ; Dong et al., 2024 ) , online AI feedback ( Guo et al., 2024 ) and Self-Rewarding LMs ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) regenerate preference data from the current policy each round. Tang et al. (2024) find that the advantage of online over offline alignment is not explained by data coverage or quality alone and point to on-policy sampling as the deciding factor; Lanchantin et al. (2025) find that semi-online training, in which the response generator is synchronized with the policy only every few updates, as in DNO-Prct’s per-iteration sampling, performs on par with fully online training and well above offline methods. SPIN ( Chen et al., 2024 ) treats the SFT targets as always preferred over self-generated responses. Game-theoretic methods seek the Nash equilibrium of the preference game: Nash-MD ( Munos et al., 2024 ) , online IPO ( Calandriello et al., 2024 ) , SPO ( Swamy et al., 2024 ) , SPPO ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , INPO ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) , DNO ( Rosset et al., 2024 ) and, concurrently with or after our experiments, MPO ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , optimistic online mirror descent ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) and RSPO ( Tang et al., 2026 ) . REBEL ( Gao et al., 2024 ) regresses relative rewards and extends to intransitive preferences, and Zhang et al. (2025c) learn general preference models beyond Bradley–Terry for such methods. INPO reaches 42.6% LC on AlpacaEval 2.0 from a Llama-3-8B SFT model with an open-weight pairwise preference model and no proprietary model in the loop. We have not found a published independent re-implementation of DNO-Prct on other base models, nor a public implementation of it. Where do the gains of AI feedback come from? Sharma et al. (2024) show that improvements attributed to reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) are largely explained by using a weaker teacher for SFT than the critic used for feedback, and that SFT directly on GPT-4 completions outperforms the pipelines they study. Our gold-response ablation (Section 6.3 ) is related but not a replication of their comparison: we did not run a matched-teacher SFT control. Ivison et al. (2024) disentangle preference data, learning algorithm, reward model and policy prompts in a comparable empirical study of DPO and PPO. Open-weight models trained specifically as evaluators can match or exceed GPT-4 on reward-model benchmarks ( Wang et al., 2024 ) ; our open-weight annotators were not evaluator-trained and retained 62–82% of the LC gain of the GPT-4o-annotated runs against GPT-4o (Section 5.4 ). LLM-as-a-judge evaluation and its failure modes: We evaluate with AlpacaEval 2.0 ( Li et al., 2023 ) and its length-controlled win rate ( Dubois et al., 2024 ) , which with the default judge and reference correlates strongly with the rankings of Chatbot Arena ( Chiang et al., 2024 ) ; our judge and references are not the default (Section 4.1 ). LLM judges exhibit position, verbosity and self-preference biases ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Panickssery et al., 2024 ; Wataoka et al., 2024 ) . Li et al. (2026) find that a judge favors students trained on data from a related model: their average preference-leakage score is about 24% when judge and data generator are the same model, as GPT-4o is in our main runs, and about 3–9% when they share a model family. Zheng et al. (2025) show that a null model that always returns the same, adversarially crafted response reaches 86.5% LC on AlpacaEval 2.0. Both appeared during or after our experiments, and Section 8 uses them to interpret our results. 3.1 Relation to Online DPO DNO is conceptually close to online DPO ( Guo et al., 2024 ) . In each round of online DPO the model generates two candidate responses to a prompt, an annotator decides which is better, and the resulting pair is used for a DPO-style update. DNO likewise samples candidates, rates them and learns from the resulting preferences, but differs in three ways. (1) Rating guideline and margin: DNO rates responses against an explicit rubric and forms a pair only when the positive–negative rating margin is sufficiently large. The margin filter is what allows the regression objective of Eq. ( 5 ) to be approximated by the pure contrastive loss without an excessively large KL coefficient ( Rosset et al., 2024 , Section 4) ; it is an approximation device rather than a condition for Nash convergence. Its empirical effect is studied in Section 6.2 . (2) Multiple on-policy candidates: Instead of a single pair per prompt, DNO samples K K candidates per prompt, intended to cover more of the policy’s output distribution than a single pair. Section 6.1 varies K K . (3) Teacher responses as candidates: DNO adds the teacher’s response y gold y^{\mathrm{gold}} to the candidate set. Rating teacher and student responses together captures cases where the student outperforms the teacher, which SPIN-style self-play ignores (Sections 6.3 and 6.4 ). Online DPO as instantiated by Guo et al. (2024) additionally keeps a fixed reference policy and samples pairs per mini-batch, whereas DNO-Prct collects a large batch per iteration, resets the reference to π t \pi_{t} , and mixes in look-back data. 4 Experimental Setup 4.1 General Setup Timeline: All experiments were run between the release of Llama 3.1 and Mistral Large 2 in late July 2024 and the end of December 2024, with the model and API versions available then. All reported results come from these 2024 runs; a few descriptive statistics, such as the prompt overlap and the truncation rate, were computed afterwards from their stored outputs. Dataset: We use the UltraFeedback dataset ( Cui et al., 2024 ; OpenBMB, 2023 ) as the fine-tuning and preference-alignment dataset. items.raw_text: Aligning Language Models with General Preferences: An Empirical Study of Direct Nash Optimization Austin Tsai Affiliation: Synopsys, Inc., Sunnyvale, CA, USA Saurav Nanda Affiliation: Synopsys, Inc., Sunnyvale, CA, USA Ganapathy Parthasarathy Affiliation: Synopsys, Inc., Sunnyvale, CA, USA Bhuvnesh Kumar Affiliation: Synopsys, Inc., Sunnyvale, CA, USA Correspondence to: bhuvnesh@synopsys.com Parivesh Choudhary Affiliation: Synopsys, Inc., Sunnyvale, CA, USA Abstract Direct Nash Optimization (DNO) aligns a language model to a general preference function by approximating the Nash equilibrium of a two-player preference game. Its practical variant, DNO-Prct, iterates on-policy sampling, LLM-based rating of the samples together with a teacher’s gold response, large-margin preference-pair selection and a DPO-style contrastive update. We re-implement DNO-Prct independently and study it on two open-weight instruct models, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1, with GPT-4o or a larger open-weight model of the same family as the annotator. On AlpacaEval 2.0 with GPT-4o as judge, three iterations raise the length-controlled (LC) win rate against GPT-4o from 31.7% to 45.3% for Llama and from 6.8% to 18.4% for Mistral, and the tuned 8B model scores above Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on every reported win rate. With same-family open-weight annotators, the runs retain 62% (Llama) and 82% (Mistral) of the LC gain achieved with GPT-4o as annotator, so the rating step does not require a proprietary model. In a separate ablation configuration, variants that remove the gold responses, remove the data look-back, or accept only teacher-preferred pairs score 6 to 10 LC points below the full procedure, whereas varying the number of on-policy samples per prompt (1 to 7) moves the LC win rate by at most 2.1 points, and a margin sweep (1 to 5) run in its own pipeline by at most 2.4 points. We also report the cost of the pipeline and where the practical algorithm departs from the theory it approximates. All results are single runs, and GPT-4o is both the teacher and the evaluation judge; we discuss what this implies for the reported gains. Keywords: RLHF, preference optimization, Direct Nash Optimization, DPO, LLM alignment, AlpacaEval, LLM-as-a-judge † † affiliationnotice: Work done while all authors were at Synopsys, Inc. 1 Introduction Pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly ( Radford et al., 2018 ; Radford et al., 2019 ; Brown et al., 2020 ; Rae et al., 2021 ) . Trained only to predict the next token, they are not by themselves aligned with what humans prefer. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) ( Christiano et al., 2017 ; Stiennon et al., 2020 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Bai et al., 2022 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; OpenAI, 2023 ) bridges this gap by collecting human preferences, training a reward model on them, and optimizing the policy with reinforcement learning. Single-stage contrastive methods such as Direct Preference Optimization ( Rafailov et al., 2023 , DPO;) remove the explicit reward model. In their standard formulations, both assume a pointwise (Bradley–Terry) reward and therefore cannot represent intransitive preferences, which Liu et al. (2025) show arise with high probability under a Luce-type preference model; they are also vulnerable to reward hacking ( Amodei et al., 2016 ) , and a reward model or preference dataset fixed in advance becomes stale as the policy distribution shifts during training ( Ross et al., 2011 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ; Azar et al., 2024 ; Munos et al., 2024 ) . To address these limitations, a line of work optimizes the general preference function directly by finding the Nash equilibrium of a two-player game, solving that game with single-player (self-play) algorithms that exploit the symmetry of the preference function ( Munos et al., 2024 ; Swamy et al., 2024 ) . For a preference function with 𝒫 ⁡ ( y ≻ y ′ ∣ x ) + 𝒫 ⁡ ( y ′ ≻ y ∣ x ) = 1 \mathcal{P}(y\succ y^{\prime}\mid x)+\mathcal{P}(y^{\prime}\succ y\mid x)=1 and 𝒫 ( π ≻ π ′ ) := 𝔼 x ∼ ρ , y ∼ π ( ⋅ ∣ x ) , y ′ ∼ π ′ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) [ 𝒫 ( y ≻ y ′ ∣ x ) ] \mathcal{P}(\pi\succ\pi^{\prime}):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\rho,\,y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x),\,y^{\prime}\sim\pi^{\prime}(\cdot\mid x)}[\mathcal{P}(y\succ y^{\prime}\mid x)] for a prompt distribution ρ \rho , a Nash equilibrium is a policy π ⋆ \pi^{\star} with 𝒫 ⁡ ( π ⋆ ≻ π ) ≥ 1 2 \mathcal{P}(\pi^{\star}\succ\pi)\geq\tfrac{1}{2} for every competing policy π \pi in the policy class Π \Pi ; this policy is the Minimax Winner of the game. Rosset et al. (2024) propose Direct Nash Optimization (DNO): a provable algorithm whose iterates converge to the Nash equilibrium on average, together with a practical variant, DNO-Prct, which in their largest run, on about ten times more prompts over six iterations, brought a 7B model to a 33% length-controlled AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate against GPT-4 Turbo, with GPT-4 Turbo as annotator and gold-response source. DNO-Prct bundles several design choices: batched on-policy sampling, a teacher’s gold response among the candidates, LLM-based rating against a rubric, a minimum rating margin, and a decaying look-back over earlier pairs. To our knowledge no independent re-implementation of DNO-Prct has been published: its published results, including its ablations, use one base model and a proprietary annotator, so it is not known whether its gains and design choices transfer to other base models and annotators. This paper is an empirical study of DNO-Prct. We re-implemented the algorithm from the description in Rosset et al. (2024) , ran it on two open-weight instruct models with GPT-4o and with same-family open-weight models as annotators, and examined its main design choices. Throughout, “DNO” refers to DNO-Prct unless stated otherwise. Our contributions are as follows. (1) An independent re-implementation with a procedural description: We give the pair-construction procedure as pseudo-code (Appendix C ), the rating prompt verbatim (Appendix A ) and the hyperparameters and implementation settings (Appendix B ). Together with Rosset et al. (2024) , this describes the pipeline in enough detail to re-implement it. (2) Gains on two model families: Over three iterations the student’s length-controlled (LC) AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate against GPT-4o rises from 31.71% to 45.32% for Llama 3.1 8B Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) and from 6.77% to 18.44% for Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1 ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) . Under the same protocol, the tuned 8B model scores above Llama 3.1 70B Instruct, which has nearly nine times as many parameters, on all four reported win rates, and the tuned 7B model narrows its gap to Mixtral 8x7B Instruct v0.1 ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) on all four, to between 0.2 and 12.8 points (Section 5.3 ). (3) Open-weight annotators: Replacing GPT-4o with Llama 3.1 70B Instruct or Mistral Large 2 as the annotator retains 62% (Llama) and 82% (Mistral) of the LC gain against the GPT-4o opponent; against GPT-4-0613 the Llama run retains 45% and the Mistral run matches the GPT-4o-annotated run, so the rating step does not require a proprietary model (Section 5.4 ). (4) Which components matter: In a separate ablation configuration, variants that remove the gold responses, remove the data look-back, or restrict pair selection to teacher-preferred pairs score 6 to 10 LC points below the full procedure against GPT-4o (9 to 19 points against GPT-4-0613), whereas the number of on-policy samples per prompt (1 to 7) moves the LC win rate against GPT-4o by at most 2.1 points, and a margin sweep (1 to 5) run in its own pipeline by at most 2.4 points (Section 6 ). We also document the cost of the pipeline (Section 7 ) and the places where DNO-Prct departs from the theory it approximates (Section 6.6 ). Rosset et al. (2024, Section 5.2) compared large-margin filtering, on-policy sampling and the SPIN and DNO-Restrictive pair rules in their own setting, and their Table 2 tracks teacher- and student-preferred pairs and the average teacher and student ratings across iterations. We extend these analyses beyond that setting, to two further base models and to open-weight annotators, add sweeps of the rating margin and the number of samples, and repeat their teacher–student analysis (Section 6.5 ). The experiments were run in 2024, and Section 3 relates them to work that appeared during or after them, notably on preference leakage between data generator and judge ( Li et al., 2026 ) and on the exploitability of AlpacaEval ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . 2 Preliminaries: Direct Nash Optimization There are two variants of Direct Nash Optimization: the theoretical DNO (Algorithm 1 ) and the practical DNO-Prct. Rosset et al. (2024) , and Munos et al. (2024) establish last-iterate convergence for the regularized game. Rosset et al. (2024) also establish two further properties (their Section 3.1 and Theorem 1). These statements hold under the assumptions of the cited results (realizability of the soft-policy-iteration target in the policy class, and boundedness), and the bound is informative only when the concentrability coefficient is small; neither condition is guaranteed for a neural policy class. The improvement is against the previous iterate under 𝒫 \mathcal{P} and ρ \rho ; it is not a statement that benchmark scores rise at every iteration or that the student surpasses a fixed teacher. The practical procedure below, with finite samples, LLM ratings, margin filtering, look-back and a single selected checkpoint, approximates the exact update and does not inherit these guarantees. DNO-Prct: The main obstacle in practice is the expectation in Eq. ( 1 ). Rosset et al. (2024) therefore propose DNO-Prct, each iteration of which has three steps: 1. Batched on-policy sampling and rating: K K outputs per prompt are sampled from the current policy π t \pi_{t} and, together with a gold response y gold y^{\mathrm{gold}} from a stronger teacher model, are scored by an annotator; the scores serve as a proxy for the pairwise win-rate ranking under 𝒫 \mathcal{P} . 2. Preference pair construction: Only pairs whose scores differ by a sufficiently large margin are kept, with the intent that the target σ ⁡ ( Δ t ⋆ ) \sigma(\Delta^{\star}_{t}) , after a rescaling of r t r_{t} , be close to one so that Eq. ( 5 ) reduces approximately to the pure contrastive (DPO) loss (an approximation discussed in Section 6.6 ); a decaying fraction of pairs from earlier iterations is mixed in (data look-back, described in Section 5.1 of Rosset et al. (2024) rather than in their Algorithm 2). 3. Contrastive update: The policy is trained with the DPO objective on the constructed pairs, with π t \pi_{t} as the reference policy. DNO-Prct is thus an iterative, on-policy form of DPO with the same contrastive objective; the difference lies in how the preference pairs are constructed (Figure 1 in Section 4.2 ). We refer readers to Rosset et al. (2024) for the derivation. 3 Related Work RLHF and offline contrastive alignment: The reward-model-plus-RL recipe ( Christiano et al., 2017 ; Stiennon et al., 2020 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Bai et al., 2022 ) is a standard route to aligned chat models. Offline contrastive methods such as DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , IPO ( Azar et al., 2024 ) and SimPO ( Meng et al., 2024 ) fit the policy directly to a preference dataset; Zephyr ( Tunstall et al., 2023 ) popularized distilled supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on UltraChat followed by DPO on UltraFeedback ( Cui et al., 2024 ) . DPO and SimPO inherit the transitivity of a pointwise (Bradley–Terry) reward, which IPO avoids, and DPO in particular is known to exploit response length ( Park et al., 2024 ) . Meng et al. (2024) report that Llama-3-8B-Instruct trained with SimPO reaches 44.7% LC on the public AlpacaEval 2.0 leaderboard, above Llama-3-70B-Instruct (34.4%), so a small model scoring above a larger sibling on this metric is not by itself evidence of a better algorithm. Iterative, online and self-play alignment: Iterative DPO ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Xiong et al., 2024 ; Dong et al., 2024 ) , online AI feedback ( Guo et al., 2024 ) and Self-Rewarding LMs ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) regenerate preference data from the current policy each round. Tang et al. (2024) find that the advantage of online over offline alignment is not explained by data coverage or quality alone and point to on-policy sampling as the deciding factor; Lanchantin et al. (2025) find that semi-online training, in which the response generator is synchronized with the policy only every few updates, as in DNO-Prct’s per-iteration sampling, performs on par with fully online training and well above offline methods. SPIN ( Chen et al., 2024 ) treats the SFT targets as always preferred over self-generated responses. Game-theoretic methods seek the Nash equilibrium of the preference game: Nash-MD ( Munos et al., 2024 ) , online IPO ( Calandriello et al., 2024 ) , SPO ( Swamy et al., 2024 ) , SPPO ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , INPO ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) , DNO ( Rosset et al., 2024 ) and, concurrently with or after our experiments, MPO ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , optimistic online mirror descent ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) and RSPO ( Tang et al., 2026 ) . REBEL ( Gao et al., 2024 ) regresses relative rewards and extends to intransitive preferences, and Zhang et al. (2025c) learn general preference models beyond Bradley–Terry for such methods. INPO reaches 42.6% LC on AlpacaEval 2.0 from a Llama-3-8B SFT model with an open-weight pairwise preference model and no proprietary model in the loop. We have not found a published independent re-implementation of DNO-Prct on other base models, nor a public implementation of it. Where do the gains of AI feedback come from? Sharma et al. (2024) show that improvements attributed to reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) are largely explained by using a weaker teacher for SFT than the critic used for feedback, and that SFT directly on GPT-4 completions outperforms the pipelines they study. Our gold-response ablation (Section 6.3 ) is related but not a replication of their comparison: we did not run a matched-teacher SFT control. Ivison et al. (2024) disentangle preference data, learning algorithm, reward model and policy prompts in a comparable empirical study of DPO and PPO. Open-weight models trained specifically as evaluators can match or exceed GPT-4 on reward-model benchmarks ( Wang et al., 2024 ) ; our open-weight annotators were not evaluator-trained and retained 62–82% of the LC gain of the GPT-4o-annotated runs against GPT-4o (Section 5.4 ). LLM-as-a-judge evaluation and its failure modes: We evaluate with AlpacaEval 2.0 ( Li et al., 2023 ) and its length-controlled win rate ( Dubois et al., 2024 ) , which with the default judge and reference correlates strongly with the rankings of Chatbot Arena ( Chiang et al., 2024 ) ; our judge and references are not the default (Section 4.1 ). LLM judges exhibit position, verbosity and self-preference biases ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Panickssery et al., 2024 ; Wataoka et al., 2024 ) . Li et al. (2026) find that a judge favors students trained on data from a related model: their average preference-leakage score is about 24% when judge and data generator are the same model, as GPT-4o is in our main runs, and about 3–9% when they share a model family. Zheng et al. (2025) show that a null model that always returns the same, adversarially crafted response reaches 86.5% LC on AlpacaEval 2.0. Both appeared during or after our experiments, and Section 8 uses them to interpret our results. 3.1 Relation to Online DPO DNO is conceptually close to online DPO ( Guo et al., 2024 ) . In each round of online DPO the model generates two candidate responses to a prompt, an annotator decides which is better, and the resulting pair is used for a DPO-style update. DNO likewise samples candidates, rates them and learns from the resulting preferences, but differs in three ways. (1) Rating guideline and margin: DNO rates responses against an explicit rubric and forms a pair only when the positive–negative rating margin is sufficiently large. The margin filter is what allows the regression objective of Eq. ( 5 ) to be approximated by the pure contrastive loss without an excessively large KL coefficient ( Rosset et al., 2024 , Section 4) ; it is an approximation device rather than a condition for Nash convergence. Its empirical effect is studied in Section 6.2 . (2) Multiple on-policy candidates: Instead of a single pair per prompt, DNO samples K K candidates per prompt, intended to cover more of the policy’s output distribution than a single pair. Section 6.1 varies K K . (3) Teacher responses as candidates: DNO adds the teacher’s response y gold y^{\mathrm{gold}} to the candidate set. Rating teacher and student responses together captures cases where the student outperforms the teacher, which SPIN-style self-play ignores (Sections 6.3 and 6.4 ). Online DPO as instantiated by Guo et al. (2024) additionally keeps a fixed reference policy and samples pairs per mini-batch, whereas DNO-Prct collects a large batch per iteration, resets the reference to π t \pi_{t} , and mixes in look-back data. 4 Experimental Setup 4.1 General Setup Timeline: All experiments were run between the release of Llama 3.1 and Mistral Large 2 in late July 2024 and the end of December 2024, with the model and API versions available then. All reported results come from these 2024 runs; a few descriptive statistics, such as the prompt overlap and the truncation rate, were computed afterwards from their stored outputs. The prompts are sourced from UltraChat, ShareGPT, Evol-Instruct, TruthfulQA, FalseQA and FLAN. The SFT and offline-DPO thresholds below are applied to the average of the four per-aspect ratings. In addition to the original content, we generate one response from GPT-4o ( OpenAI, 2024 ) for every prompt to serve as the gold response y gold y^{\mathrm{gold}} in the GPT-4o-annotated runs. Base models and annotators: We experiment with two base models, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1. The base model provides the initial weights for every run except the two-stage runs of Section 5.5 and the look-back ablation of Section 6.4 , which start from an SFT checkpoint. GPT-4o is the annotator in the DNO experiments except those of Section 5.4 , where the annotator is Llama 3.1 70B Instruct or Mistral Large 2 ( Mistral AI, 2024 , Mistral-Large-Instruct-2407, 123B parameters; hereafter Mistral Large;) . items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.05346 (cs) [Submitted on 3 Nov 2026] Title: Agnostic Learning by Imitating Authors: Sílvia Casacuberta , Parikshit Gopalan , Varun Kanade , Omer Reingold , Konstantinos Stavropoulos , Pranay Tankala View a PDF of the paper titled Agnostic Learning by Imitating, by S\'ilvia Casacuberta and Parikshit Gopalan and Varun Kanade and Omer Reingold and Konstantinos Stavropoulos and Pranay Tankala View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Given a class of machine learning models and sample access to a data distribution with binary labels, which computational task is harder: training a discriminative model that distinguishes positive and negative labels as well as the best member of the class, or training a generative model whose outputs are indistinguishable from real data by all members of the class? We prove that these two fundamental tasks in computational learning theory are not just closely related, but actually equivalent to each other in complexity. One direction of this equivalence was previously known. Indeed, the powerful regularity lemma in complexity theory gives an efficient oracle reduction from the indistinguishability task (a.k.a. multiaccuracy) to the distinguishing task (a.k.a. agnostic learning) in the style of boosting algorithms. Our main contribution is an efficient oracle reduction in the other direction. Taking this idea further, we show that a multiaccuracy oracle is a remarkably powerful primitive, achieving not just agnostic learning but also a wide range of seemingly more demanding learning objectives via similarly efficient and direct constructions. Our results crucially use the power of making adaptive queries to the oracle, and stand in stark contrast to prior work, which showed that post-processing a single multiaccurate predictor is insufficient for even weak forms of learning. On a technical level, we draw a connection between our (offline) problem and a version of no-regret learning in the online setting, which allows us to use follow-the-leader type algorithms to modify the label distribution and aggregate the predictions of the multiaccuracy oracle. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.05325 (cs) [Submitted on 3 Nov 2026] Title: CATF: A Manager-Worker Framework for Context-Aware Time-Series Forecasting Authors: Yueqiao Chen , Dongyu Liu View a PDF of the paper titled CATF: A Manager-Worker Framework for Context-Aware Time-Series Forecasting, by Yueqiao Chen and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: We study context-aware time-series forecasting, in which a single target variable is predicted from its own history and a set of contextual variables, such as weather and calendar information. As the context becomes more diverse, a single model struggles to capture all of its regimes, while ensemble learning and Mixture-of-Experts approaches rely on manual data partitioning or soft routing, which increases the inference cost and hinders interpretability. We propose CATF, a Context-Aware Time-Series Forecasting framework built on a Manager-Worker architecture: a Transformer-based Manager routes each input to a single Worker based on the context, using hard routing during both training and inference. The Workers thus specialize without manual data partitioning, and any single-model forecaster can serve as a Worker. On five context-rich datasets, four horizons, and two normalization schemes, CATF improves over its standalone counterpart in 162 of 200 comparisons, the best CATF-enhanced model outperforms the best standalone baseline in 19 of 20 settings, and it outperforms the zero-shot Time-MoE foundation model in 15 of 20 settings. A case study on bike-sharing data shows that the Manager routes inputs by the calendar and that each Worker specializes in a different weekly pattern. items.content: CATF : A Manager-Worker Framework for Context-Aware Time-Series Forecasting Yueqiao Chen Affiliation: UC Davis , Davis , CA , USA email: yeqchen@ucdavis.edu and Dongyu Liu Affiliation: UC Davis , Davis , CA , USA email: dyuliu@ucdavis.edu © none Abstract. We study context-aware time-series forecasting, in which a single target variable is predicted from its own history and a set of contextual variables, such as weather and calendar information. As the context becomes more diverse, a single model struggles to capture all of its regimes, while ensemble learning and Mixture-of-Experts approaches rely on manual data partitioning or soft routing, which increases the inference cost and hinders interpretability. We propose CATF , a C ontext- A ware T ime-Series F orecasting framework built on a Manager-Worker architecture: a Transformer-based Manager routes each input to a single Worker based on the context, using hard routing during both training and inference. The Workers thus specialize without manual data partitioning, and any single-model forecaster can serve as a Worker. On five context-rich datasets, four horizons, and two normalization schemes, CATF improves over its standalone counterpart in 162 of 200 comparisons, the best CATF -enhanced model outperforms the best standalone baseline in 19 of 20 settings, and it outperforms the zero-shot Time-MoE foundation model in 15 of 20 settings. A case study on bike-sharing data shows that the Manager routes inputs by the calendar and that each Worker specializes in a different weekly pattern. Keywords: Time-series Forecasting, Context-aware Learning, Exogenous Variables, Training Algorithm, Manager-Worker Architecture, Deep Learning 1. Introduction Time-series forecasting is critical to applications such as weather prediction, electricity load management, traffic analysis, financial forecasting, and industrial monitoring ( Wu et al., 2023b ; Weron, 2014 ; Lv et al., 2014 ; Ariyo et al., 2014 ; Alnegheimish et al., 2022 ) . However, growing temporal complexity and rich contextual dependencies make accurate forecasting increasingly difficult and computationally expensive. Contextual variables are often heterogeneous and dynamic, evolving abruptly or nonlinearly over time. For example, hourly bike-sharing demand depends on weather, temperature, and the calendar: on working days it peaks during the morning and evening commutes, whereas on weekends and holidays it follows a single midday peak, and a holiday on a weekday can switch the demand to the weekend pattern. In this work, we focus on such context-aware forecasting: the goal is to forecast a single target variable from its history and the contextual variables that drive it, a setting also known as forecasting with exogenous variables. This differs from the setting of most multivariate forecasting benchmarks ( thu, [n. d.] ) , in which all variables are forecast jointly; here, the contextual variables serve only as inputs. Recent advances in deep learning have led to impressive results in time-series forecasting. Convolutional networks ( Wu et al., 2023a ) , graph neural networks ( Huang et al., 2023 ) , and Transformer-based models ( Liu et al., 2024a ) models have been adapted to capture complex temporal dependencies. More recently, large-scale time-series foundation models (TSFMs) ( Jin et al., 2024 ; Qiao et al., 2025 ) have shown strong performance in zero-shot and few-shot settings. However, these models are expensive to fine-tune, struggle with distribution shifts, and often fail to generalize to domain-specific dynamics. To improve adaptability, researchers have explored alternatives such as retrieval-augmented forecasting ( Liu et al., 2024b ) , meta learning ( Oreshkin et al., 2021 ) , and adaptive policies ( Fu et al., 2022 ) . Hybrid forecasting approaches offer another promising direction by allowing model specialization under diverse conditions. Ensemble methods ( Galicia et al., 2019 ; He et al., 2023 ) train specialized models on partitioned subsets and aggregate their predictions. However, they incur inference overhead and require manual segmentation and weighting strategies. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models ( Jordan and Jacobs, 1996 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) improve efficiency through sparse activation but demand careful gating design and are prone to expert under-utilization without strong regularization . To address these challenges, we propose CATF , a C ontext- A ware T ime-Series F orecasting framework based on a Manager-Worker (MW) architecture. CATF consists of a high-level transformer-based Manager and a set of Worker models trained via joint optimization. The Manager dynamically routes each input to a single specialized Worker based on contextual features, enabling each Worker to focus on a distinct subset of conditions. Inspired by economic specialization ( Hidalgo, 2021 ) , we formulate training as a competitive yet cooperative process: the Manager learns to assign inputs to the most suitable Worker, while Workers specialize in minimizing error within their assigned contexts. Unlike conventional MoEs, CATF employs hard routing , assigning each input to a single Worker during both training and inference. This improves interpretability, encourages Worker specialization, and eliminates the need for manual partitioning or complex gating mechanisms. In addition, CATF supports heterogeneous architectures, enabling seamless integration of state-of-the-art forecasting models with minimal tuning. We evaluated CATF on five real-world context-rich datasets across four forecasting horizons, observed improvements over strong single-model baselines, and analyze its routing decisions. Our key contributions are as follows. • Modular framework. We propose CATF , a Manager-Worker framework in which a Transformer-based Manager routes each input to one of several Worker models through hard routing, trained with a joint mechanism that lets the Workers specialize without manual data partitioning (Section 4 ). CATF is model-agnostic: any single-model forecaster can serve as a Worker without modification, in homogeneous or heterogeneous configurations, and we instantiate it with five representative architectures, Autoformer ( Wu et al., 2021 ) , Informer ( Zhou et al., 2021 ) , FEDformer ( Zhou et al., 2022 ) , TimesNet ( Wu et al., 2023a ) , and iTransformer ( Liu et al., 2024a ) . • Context-aware interpretation. Because each prediction is produced by a single, identifiable Worker, the routing decisions can be inspected and related to the context. In a case study on a real-world bike-sharing dataset, we show that the Manager learns to route inputs by the most relevant contextual variables (e.g., working days vs. weekends) and that the Workers specialize accordingly (Section 6 ); on synthetic data with known context-driven regimes, the same analysis recovers the ground truth (Appendix D.2 ). • Performance improvement. On five context-rich real-world datasets, four horizons, and two normalization schemes, CATF improves over its standalone counterpart in 162 of the 200 comparisons (81%), the best CATF -enhanced model outperforms the best standalone baseline in 19 of the 20 settings, CATF reduces the run-to-run variance of unstable baselines, and it outperforms the zero-shot Time-MoE foundation model ( Shi et al., 2025 ) in 15 of the 20 settings (Section 5.2 ). 2. Related Work 2.1. Time Series Forecasting Single-Model Approaches. Early forecasting models relied on convolutional (CNN) ( Bai et al., 2018 ; Dempster et al., 2019 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2023a ) and recurrent (RNN) ( Zhao et al., 2017 ; Rangapuram et al., 2018 ; Salinas et al., 2020 ) architectures to capture temporal dependencies. CNNs are efficient and effective for local patterns, while RNNs model autoregressive behavior. However, both struggle with long-range dependencies. Graph neural networks (GNNs) ( Wu et al., 2020 ; Huang et al., 2023 ) address inter-variable relationships but incur high computational cost in high-dimensional or long-sequence settings. More recently, multilayer perceptron (MLP) models ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2023 ) have emerged as efficient alternatives, relying on token mixing or linear projections. Transformer-based models ( Zhou et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2021 ; Zhou et al., 2022 ; Nie et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024a ) have become more popular due to their ability to model global dependencies through self-attention. Despite their strengths, single-model architectures often struggle to generalize across heterogeneous and dynamic temporal regimes. Models tuned for specific conditions may underperform under unexpected shifts such as holidays or extreme events. Our proposed framework addresses this limitation by enabling dynamic model selection based on contextual cues. Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs). These approaches aim to build universal forecasting models pretrained on large-scale datasets ( Liang et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2024 ) . These models vary in architecture (e.g., Transformer, diffusion, or MLP), pretraining objectives (supervised or self-supervised), and downstream adaptation strategies (fine-tuning, prompting, zero-shot) ( Goswami et al., 2024 ; Ansari et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024c ; Das et al., 2024b ; Das et al., 2024a ; Gao et al., 2024 ; Benechehab et al., 2025 ) . Introduction Time-series forecasting is critical to applications such as weather prediction, electricity load management, traffic analysis, financial forecasting, and industrial monitoring ( Wu et al., 2023b ; Weron, 2014 ; Lv et al., 2014 ; Ariyo et al., 2014 ; Alnegheimish et al., 2022 ) . However, growing temporal complexity and rich contextual dependencies make accurate forecasting increasingly difficult and computationally expensive. Contextual variables are often heterogeneous and dynamic, evolving abruptly or nonlinearly over time. For example, hourly bike-sharing demand depends on weather, temperature, and the calendar: on working days it peaks during the morning and evening commutes, whereas on weekends and holidays it follows a single midday peak, and a holiday on a weekday can switch the demand to the weekend pattern. In this work, we focus on such context-aware forecasting: the goal is to forecast a single target variable from its history and the contextual variables that drive it, a setting also known as forecasting with exogenous variables. This differs from the setting of most multivariate forecasting benchmarks ( thu, [n. d.] ) , in which all variables are forecast jointly; here, the contextual variables serve only as inputs. Recent advances in deep learning have led to impressive results in time-series forecasting. Convolutional networks ( Wu et al., 2023a ) , graph neural networks ( Huang et al., 2023 ) , and Transformer-based models ( Liu et al., 2024a ) models have been adapted to capture complex temporal dependencies. More recently, large-scale time-series foundation models (TSFMs) ( Jin et al., 2024 ; Qiao et al., 2025 ) have shown strong performance in zero-shot and few-shot settings. However, these models are expensive to fine-tune, struggle with distribution shifts, and often fail to generalize to domain-specific dynamics. To improve adaptability, researchers have explored alternatives such as retrieval-augmented forecasting ( Liu et al., 2024b ) , meta learning ( Oreshkin et al., 2021 ) , and adaptive policies ( Fu et al., 2022 ) . Hybrid forecasting approaches offer another promising direction by allowing model specialization under diverse conditions. Ensemble methods ( Galicia et al., 2019 ; He et al., 2023 ) train specialized models on partitioned subsets and aggregate their predictions. However, they incur inference overhead and require manual segmentation and weighting strategies. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models ( Jordan and Jacobs, 1996 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) improve efficiency through sparse activation but demand careful gating design and are prone to expert under-utilization without strong regularization . To address these challenges, we propose CATF , a C ontext- A ware T ime-Series F orecasting framework based on a Manager-Worker (MW) architecture. CATF consists of a high-level transformer-based Manager and a set of Worker models trained via joint optimization. The Manager dynamically routes each input to a single specialized Worker based on contextual features, enabling each Worker to focus on a distinct subset of conditions. Inspired by economic specialization ( Hidalgo, 2021 ) , we formulate training as a competitive yet cooperative process: the Manager learns to assign inputs to the most suitable Worker, while Workers specialize in minimizing error within their assigned contexts. Unlike conventional MoEs, CATF employs hard routing , assigning each input to a single Worker during both training and inference. This improves interpretability, encourages Worker specialization, and eliminates the need for manual partitioning or complex gating mechanisms. In addition, CATF supports heterogeneous architectures, enabling seamless integration of state-of-the-art forecasting models with minimal tuning. We evaluated CATF on five real-world context-rich datasets across four forecasting horizons, observed improvements over strong single-model baselines, and analyze its routing decisions. Our key contributions are as follows. • Modular framework. We propose CATF , a Manager-Worker framework in which a Transformer-based Manager routes each input to one of several Worker models through hard routing, trained with a joint mechanism that lets the Workers specialize without manual data partitioning (Section 4 ). CATF is model-agnostic: any single-model forecaster can serve as a Worker without modification, in homogeneous or heterogeneous configurations, and we instantiate it with five representative architectures, Autoformer ( Wu et al., 2021 ) , Informer ( Zhou et al., 2021 ) , FEDformer ( Zhou et al., 2022 ) , TimesNet ( Wu et al., 2023a ) , and iTransformer ( Liu et al., 2024a ) . • Context-aware interpretation. Because each prediction is produced by a single, identifiable Worker, the routing decisions can be inspected and related to the context. In a case study on a real-world bike-sharing dataset, we show that the Manager learns to route inputs by the most relevant contextual variables (e.g., working days vs. weekends) and that the Workers specialize accordingly (Section 6 ); on synthetic data with known context-driven regimes, the same analysis recovers the ground truth (Appendix D.2 ). • Performance improvement. On five context-rich real-world datasets, four horizons, and two normalization schemes, CATF improves over its standalone counterpart in 162 of the 200 comparisons (81%), the best CATF -enhanced model outperforms the best standalone baseline in 19 of the 20 settings, CATF reduces the run-to-run variance of unstable baselines, and it outperforms the zero-shot Time-MoE foundation model ( Shi et al., 2025 ) in 15 of the 20 settings (Section 5.2 ). 2. The lower panel expands the manager into feature encoding, Transformer encoders, last-timestep pooling, decoder, and softmax. CATF consists of a manager model ℳ \mathcal{M} and K K worker models 𝒲 1 , … , 𝒲 K \mathcal{W}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{W}_{K} , as illustrated in Figure 1 a. The manager ℳ \mathcal{M} takes the target history X X and the context history C C as input and estimates, for each worker 𝒲 i \mathcal{W}_{i} , the probability P ^ i \hat{P}_{i} that it is best suited to predict the future target sequence. The worker with the highest probability, 𝒲 k ∗ \mathcal{W}_{k^{*}} with k ∗ = arg ⁡ max i ⁡ P ^ i k^{*}=\arg\max_{i}\hat{P}_{i} , is selected and generates the forecast Y ^ = 𝒲 k ∗ ​ ( X , C ) \hat{Y}=\mathcal{W}_{k^{*}}(X,C) from the same input; at inference time, the other workers are not executed. 4.1.1. Manager Model The manager performs a K K -class classification task, mapping input ( X , C ) (X,C) to a probability distribution over the K K worker models. As shown in Figure 1 b, the manager follows a Transformer-based architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , consisting of: • Feature Encoding (L1): A linear projection followed by layer normalization, ReLU activation, and dropout transforms raw input into high-dimensional embeddings. This preprocessing ensures stable training and expressive representations, which are essential for downstream temporal modeling. • Transformer Encoder Stack (L2): A stack of L m L_{m} Transformer encoder layers models long-range and complex temporal-contextual dependencies through self-attention mechanisms. Each layer consists of multi-head self-attention and position-wise feedforward sub-layers, equipped with GELU activation ( Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016 ) and residual connections. GELU is chosen for its smooth, non-linear behavior, which preserves gradient flow and has been empirically shown to enhance optimization stability and performance in deep Transformer-based networks. • Output Layer (L3–L4): Following Transformer-based classification designs ( Chen et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ) , last-timestep pooling summarizes the sequence into a fixed-length representation. This is passed through a decoder (L3) and softmax (L4) to produce the output distribution over workers. Last-timestep pooling preserves the most recent temporal information, which is critical for decision-making in time-sensitive forecasting scenarios. 4.1.2. These models also serve as baselines for evaluation. Their base implementations are consistent with the official versions provided in the Time-Series-Library ( thu, [n. d.] ) , and we use the same hyper-parameter settings to ensure fair comparisons. Only this worker is trained on the sample (step \raisebox{-0.9pt}{6}⃝; lines 9–13), while the other workers are not updated. This selective training strategy ensures that each worker is exposed to and learns from samples within specific contextual regimes. Over time, this encourages the emergence of functional specialization—each worker becomes proficient in forecasting under particular conditions. Section 6 analyzes this specialization empirically. This approach is inspired by the principle of economic specialization ( Hidalgo, 2021 ) , where agents maximize collective productivity by focusing on tasks they are best suited to. Similarly, CATF enables each worker to “do what it does best,” thereby improving overall forecasting accuracy and robustness in heterogeneous environments. Figure 2. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.05309 (cs) [Submitted on 3 Nov 2026] Title: $Φ$asmaNet: A Staged Spectral Token-Refinement Architecture for Fast Gravitational-Wave Signal-to-Noise Ratio Prediction Authors: Ioannis Tsioulis , Anastasios Tefas , Nikolaos Stergioulas View a PDF of the paper titled $\Phi$asmaNet: A Staged Spectral Token-Refinement Architecture for Fast Gravitational-Wave Signal-to-Noise Ratio Prediction, by Ioannis Tsioulis and Anastasios Tefas and Nikolaos Stergioulas View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Quantifying selection effects in gravitational-wave population studies requires millions of costly signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) calculations. We present $\Phi$asmaNet, a compact neural architecture for structured tabular regression, with staged spectral refinement as an explicit architectural prior. Learned input tokens are refined through ordered attention-based $\Phi$-Stages, each augmented by a $\Phi$-Refractor subspace-mixing module, then revisited through gated top-down $\Phi$-Feedback. Applied to the 11-dimensional parameters of precessing, higher-mode binary black hole signals (IMRPhenomXPHM), it predicts phase-averaged optimal SNR for a single detector at fixed Advanced LIGO design sensitivity. With approximately 732k parameters, it outperforms MLP, 1D-ResNet and Transformer-encoder baselines under matched training across $10^5$--$10^6$ samples. At $10^6$ samples, it achieves $100-\mathrm{MAPE}=98.73\%$ on the held-out test set, $99.29\%$ after rank-preserving monotonic (PCHIP) calibration, and $99.39\%$ ($R^2=0.9998$) in the detection-relevant regime $\rho>8$, with stable accuracy across independent dataset realizations. On a single GPU, it sustains approximately $1.2\times10^5$ SNR evaluations per second and processes a $10^6$-injection catalogue end-to-end in approximately 8.3 s, about two orders of magnitude faster than conventional waveform-and-inner-product calculations on a 16-core CPU. Exact distance rescaling through $\rho\propto1/d_L$ supports repeated catalogue-wide detectability evaluations. The fully documented pipeline is intended as a reproducible benchmark, while results on public tabular datasets indicate competitiveness beyond gravitational-wave applications. Although demonstrated for a fixed single-detector configuration, the construction supports extensions to detector networks and epoch-specific sensitivities. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.05345 (cs) [Submitted on 3 Nov 2026] Title: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning Improves Long Horizon Agents Authors: Hongyin Luo , Wei Fang , Lijie Yang , Owen Stepan , Daniel Suit , Jeff Krapf , Dana Wensberg , Jack O'Brien View a PDF of the paper titled Adversarial Speculative Reasoning Improves Long Horizon Agents, by Hongyin Luo and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Speculative decoding has been treated purely as a systems optimization that speeds up large language model decoding without changing the model behavior. Under this view, the growing effort to train better draft models has been focused solely on acceptance rate. We argue that this view does not hold true for long-horizon agent reasoning. Measuring frontier open-weight models on complex agentic tasks with different speculative decoding approaches, we found that numerical noise grows within verification windows, and the draft acceptance results of the thinking process can change the output distribution of the model after 30 steps, thus noticeably influencing the reasoning accuracy of long-horizon agents in random directions. In this work, we improve the reasoning capability of target models by controlling such noise. While we cannot change the overall token distribution verified by the target model, we can encode critical reasoning with highest precision by training the draft model to be rejected. We identify these points in agent traces and train the draft model to favor adversarial preference. At inference the trained draft and the target part ways precisely at these decision points, verification restarts, so that critical thinking tokens are sampled from the target model and encoded under its least noisy conditions. This approach makes critical reasoning better indexed and more durable over a long horizon. On complex agentic coding benchmarks, our approach raises end-to-end success rate with no change to the target model or its output distribution. Our results recast the speculative decoding mechanism from a pure accelerator into an active allocator for context precision that improves the accuracy of long-horizon agents by training 0.06% to 0.28% of hosted parameters. (2025) , and is accelerated by a DFlash2 block-diffusion draft Chen et al. (2026b) whose verification block has 8 positions. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash runs with a DSPARK draft that proposes 5 tokens per step, so each verification block has 6 positions. We index the positions of a verification block by slot s = 0 , … , W − 1 s=0,\dots,W-1 , where W W is the block width. Slot 0 holds the last committed token; slots s ≥ 1 s\geq 1 hold draft tokens. The next-token distribution computed at slot s s is the one used to verify the draft token at slot s + 1 s+1 , or to resample in its place. Error metric. For a position and two forward passes that should agree, we compare log-probabilities token by token. At each position we take the four most likely tokens under a reference pass, together with the token the trajectory actually emits, and record | Δ ​ log ⁡ p | = | log ⁡ p 1 ​ ( v ) − log ⁡ p 2 ​ ( v ) | |\Delta\log p|=|\log p_{1}(v)-\log p_{2}(v)| for each such token v v . Log-probabilities use the natural logarithm, so differences are in natural-log units ( nats ). A difference of 1 nat is a factor of e ≈ 2.7 e\approx 2.7 in probability, and 2 nats a factor of e 2 ≈ 7.4 e^{2}\approx 7.4 . We report the mean and the fraction of tokens whose difference exceeds 1, 2 or 3 nats. The tails matter because our agents sample at temperature 1 with top- p = 0.95 p=0.95 or 1.0 1.0 . In agentic reasoning, a shift of 1–2 nats in the emitted token’s log-probability changes whether that token lies inside the sampling nucleus in 12% of cases, 2–3 nats in 47%, and more than 3 nats in over 84%. 3.2 Measurement Methods Sliding-window verification. Comparing a verification pass against a separate decoding request mixes two noise sources: the forward pass of decoding, and the independent prefill that rebuilds the prefix in each request. To exclude the latter, we hold the prefix fixed in memory and repeat only the forward decode pass. We first generate a reference trajectory by greedy single-token decoding, so that the tokens under test are the target’s own choices rather than the draft’s. For each position q q of the trajectory and each slot s s , we prefill the prompt and the trajectory up to the block’s anchor q − s q-s , write the next W W trajectory tokens into the verify block, and execute that same verify forward pass R = 4 R=4 times on the unchanged key-value cache. Row s s of each repetition gives the distribution at position q q computed from slot s s . For decoding, we prefill up to q q and execute the same single-token decode step R R times. Differences between repetitions then contain only the numerical nondeterminism of one forward pass on identical inputs. We measure 1631 positions on GLM-5.3 and 1294 on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, drawn from DeepSWE prompts with 6k–24k tokens of context. Following a verify-written context over a long horizon. Method 1 measures one forward pass. An agent, however, keeps every token it writes and reads it back for the rest of the task. In each GLM-5.3 DeepSWE trajectory we select the assistant turn with the longest reasoning and call it the source turn (median of 9k tokens, after a median of 45k-token prefix). We write the source turn’s tokens into the key-value cache for two scenarios: (A) through DFlash blockwise-verification, with every source token forced and accepted through its verify slot; or (B) through single-token decoding. The token sequence is identical on both paths; only the computation that wrote its key-value entries differs. Reusing that cache, we then score the remainder of the real trajectory teacher-forced, up to 128k further tokens (a median of 95 subsequent assistant turns), and record the log-probability of every assistant token; tool outputs stay in the context but are not scored. Each path is built twice ( A , A ′ A,A^{\prime} and B , B ′ B,B^{\prime} ). Because | A − B | |A-B| contains the variance of both paths, we compare the paths through their own build-to-build deviations, | A − A ′ | |A-A^{\prime}| versus | B − B ′ | |B-B^{\prime}| , and count tokens whose log-probability moves by more than 1, 2, 3 or 4 nats. We ran this study on 96 distinct tasks and scored 6.38M scored assistant tokens per build. In summary, sliding-window verification shows the noise growth within a draft block and the latter measures the impact of the noise in long-horizon agent reasoning. 3.3 Findings Precision falls along the verification block. Figure 1 reports the decoding error by slot. On GLM-5.3, slot 0 is exactly as noisy as single-token decoding (0.473 vs. 0.478 nats). Beyond slot 0 the noise rises with every position: the slope is + 0.0195 +0.0195 nats per slot with 95% confidence interval (CI), about 4% of the slot-0 level per slot, and the last slot is 34% noisier than the first. Large deviations grow faster than the mean. Shifts beyond 2 nats rise from 3.2% of tokens at slot 0 to 6.2% at slot 7, and shifts beyond 3 nats from 1.1% to 2.1%. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash shows the same pattern. Its slot-0 noise is half that of GLM-5.3 and its tails are much thinner, but the noise grows at the same relative rate: + 0.0094 +0.0094 nats per slot), again about 4% of the slot-0 level per slot. Shifts beyond 1 nat rise from 3.1% to 4.5% ( + 1.4 +1.4 points), and beyond 2 nats from 0.41% to 0.68%. Figure 1: Single-pass numerical noise | Δ ​ log ⁡ p | |\Delta\log p| by verify slot between repeated forwards on an identical prefix. (a) Mean deviation, with the per-slot slope. (b, c) Fraction of tokens shifted by more than 1 and 2 nats (log scale). (d) Mean deviation relative to slot 0, with least-squares fits: both models grow by about 4% of their slot-0 level per slot. Slopes with 95% bootstrap CIs over positions: + 0.0195 +0.0195 [ + 0.0174 , + 0.0214 ] [+0.0174,+0.0214] (GLM-5.3) and + 0.0094 +0.0094 [ + 0.0078 , + 0.0110 ] [+0.0078,+0.0110] (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash). Observation 1. The first slot of a verification block is as precise as single-token decoding. Every later slot is less precise: numerical noise grows by roughly 4% per slot. The chance of high deviation nearly doubles by the end of a verify block. Why the noise grows. We fix the input tokens and KV cache for repeated decoding and verifications inside the forward passes. A token at slot s s attends to the key-value entries of slots 0 , … , s − 1 0,\dots,s-1 , and those entries are computed in the same launch rather than read from the cache. Each repetition recomputes them with its own rounding, and slot s s inherits the accumulated variation of all earlier slots. Slot 0 reads only cached entries, which is why it matches decoding. Verification is therefore exact in distribution but not uniform in precision: the further into a block a distribution is computed, the noisier it is. The excess is confined to the extreme tail. For deviations up to 2 nats the two paths are indistinguishable at every distance pooled over turns 11–90. Error bars are 95% bootstrap CIs over trajectories. Context written through verification reads back like decode-written context for about 30 turns and then produces significantly more extreme deviations beyond 4 nats in output token distribution of the target model. 3.4 Implications Taken together, the two measurements give a simple picture. Speculative verification preserves the target’s distribution but its precision is not uniform, and the loss of precision is structured: it grows along the verification block, concentrates in large deviations, and the encoding noises on thinking tokens can surface far downstream. This has no consequence for most tokens, which are routine and robust to small perturbations. It matters for the few tokens at which an agent commits to a decision, because those tokens shape every turn that follows. Standard speculative decoding is indifferent to where such tokens land: whether a decision is committed at the precise head of a block or at its noisy tail depends only on how many draft tokens happened to be accepted before it. The position at which a token is committed is not determined by the target, however; it is decided by the draft. If the draft proposes something the target rejects, the target resamples that position itself, and the next verification block starts from slot 0. A draft that is reliably rejected at decision points therefore moves those decisions to the most precise slot and resets the precision of the tokens that follow, without changing the output distribution. items.content: You don’t need long context Peter Belcak Saurav Muralidharan Jindong Jiang Yonggan Fu Wonmin Byeon Hanrong Ye Ryan Angilly Ali Taghibakhshi Shih-Yang Liu Siru Ouyang Greg Heinrich Pavlo Molchanov Abstract Abstract. Later tokens are costlier to generate than earlier tokens. On frontier open weight models, the disparity in cost may rise to as much as 7x. Through frequent compaction, we show across a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks that frontier language models sacrifice little to no task accuracy when maintaining short contexts. We further demonstrate that LLM performance does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even when taking at most one action per context, and based on that we outline the concept of semantic state space models (SSSMs). Our findings question the need for long-context language models. Links: Lab | Project Moonshot: Local Frontier Intelligence 1 Introduction Figure 1: The cost of long context. Dollar cost of generating 1 1 M output tokens on an existing input KV cache as a function of the context window size, obtained by converting the measured peak decode throughput of each deployment at on-demand H100 prices ( $ 3.85 \$3.85 per GPU-hour, Nebius, Sept. 2026). Input request lengths are drawn uniformly at random. GLM 5.2 and Kimi K2.6 are served with INT4 weights and BF16 activations, Qwen 3 Coder Next is served in BF16. Serving at a context window size of 256 256 K rather than 16 16 K costs 3.6 × 3.6\times more per generated token for GLM, 5.6 × 5.6\times more for Kimi, and 7 × 7\times more for Qwen. Not all tokens are generated equal. Token generation latency and memory footprint both grow with the number of tokens in a language model’s context. This is due to the inherent linear 1 1 1 Model architectures with a constant cost of token generation with respect to context depth have been repeatedly proposed but have never been fully embraced – linear-cost attention-based mechanisms remain the backbone of all popular language models. relationship between the computational cost of generating a token and its depth within a context [ 25 ] . Figure 1 shows the cloud token generation cost as a function of context window size for a selection of popular open-weight models. Observe that there is a considerable monetary benefit to serving models on cloud GPUs with consistently shorter contexts. This fact is often hidden from the end user since retail token prices are quoted at a fixed price per 1 1 M tokens regardless of the input context length. Note that the extent of cost reductions ( 3.6 × 3.6\times to 7 × 7\times ) rivals or exceeds that of many other orthogonal optimization methods such as aggressive quantization or structured sparsification [ 5 , 14 , 8 ] . Monetary cost is not the only quality of LM workloads that suffers when inputs are long. Figure 2 shows the token generation latency, throughput, and memory footprint of several popular locally-run coding models as a function of the input context length. Observe how the generation inter-token latency approximately doubles for several models across the measured context lengths, implying a doubling of the time required to generate a response at longer contexts. Put simply, the longer the input context provided to the language model (LM), the slower, more memory hungry, and more expensive its output token generation. Figure 2: The burden of long context. The token generation latency, token throughput, and memory footprint of several open-source models measured on an NVIDIA DGX Spark plotted as a function of input context length. For several models, later tokens take approximately 2x longer to generate than earlier tokens and require a larger memory footprint. Given the considerable benefits of keeping input context short in both cloud and edge LM use, one would assume that popular LMs would have naturally evolved to operate on contexts only as short as necessary to complete their tasks. This could not be farther from the truth. As seen in Table 1 , which compares the lengths of well-known works of writing with the context window sizes of representative proprietary and open-weight models, context window sizes have vastly outgrown many influential writings. It would seem that models have been evolving to accommodate the ever larger possible inputs rather than to maximize efficiency. Literary works Model context window sizes Work Words Tokens Model Words Tokens The Old Man and the Sea [ 21 ] ∼ 27 \sim 27 K ∼ 37 \sim 37 K MiniMax M2.7 [ 31 ] ∼ 150 \sim 150 K 200 200 K The Great Gatsby [ 15 ] ∼ 48 \sim 48 K ∼ 64 \sim 64 K Claude Opus 4.5 [ 2 ] ∼ 150 \sim 150 K 200 200 K Qur’an (Saheeh Int’l translation) [ 38 ] ∼ 156 \sim 156 K ∼ 207 \sim 207 K Gemma 4 31B [ 16 ] ∼ 192 \sim 192 K 256 256 K King James New Testament [ 26 ] ∼ 181 \sim 181 K ∼ 241 \sim 241 K Kimi K2.6 [ 32 ] ∼ 192 \sim 192 K 256 256 K Great Expectations [ 12 ] ∼ 184 \sim 184 K ∼ 245 \sim 245 K Qwen 3 Coder Next [ 9 ] ∼ 197 \sim 197 K 262 262 K The Lord of the Rings [ 42 ] ∼ 481 \sim 481 K ∼ 640 \sim 640 K Gemini 3.8 Flash [ 13 ] ∼ 750 \sim 750 K 1 1 M War and Peace [ 43 ] ∼ 566 \sim 566 K ∼ 753 \sim 753 K GLM 5.2 [ 51 ] ∼ 750 \sim 750 K 1 1 M King James Old Testament [ 26 ] ∼ 603 \sim 603 K ∼ 802 \sim 802 K GPT 5.6 Sol [ 35 ] ∼ 790 \sim 790 K 1.05 1.05 M Table 1: Lengths of literary works against model context window sizes. Word counts use the cited English editions. Word-token conversions use approximately 1.33 1.33 tokens per English word, while actual counts vary with text and tokenizer. Models and their context window sizes are detailed in Section 2.3 . The enormous context window sizes of contemporary LMs and the tangible cost advantages of keeping their contexts short thus appear to be at odds with each other. While operating with longer contexts might in some cases be thought beneficial to model task accuracy, we must ask: RQ0 Are long contexts necessary ? If not, let’s do away with long contexts and long-context models. And, if there are currently any objective benefits of keeping long context models, we can likely preserve them by making the appropriate post-training adjustments to future models. To answer 0 , look at where the so-called long contexts (and, correspondingly, large context windows) in language modeling come from. Broadly, there are two types of workloads that often result in long input contexts being passed to LMs: LCW1 Workloads of long-horizon tasks – tasks that may require many actions in order to be completed and where the context builds up as the model makes its way towards the completion of the task [ 11 , 47 , 52 ] . LCW2 Workloads of long-input tasks – tasks that require operating across a large amount of input information [ 6 , 45 , 29 ] . Examining these two types of workloads more closely, it is not immediately clear whether operating on long contexts is necessary in order to complete them. In particular, the entire conversational history of 1 does not necessarily need to be considered at every step of a long-horizon operation in order to successfully complete the task. Likewise, the long inputs of 2 do not necessarily need to be ingested in their entirety at all times in order for the workload to conclude successfully. Moreover, observe that the tasks in 2 can always be reduced to 1 by storing the long input as a resource and equipping the LM with a tool for selective input reading. Motivated by the advantages of keeping LM generation contexts short and the apparent lack of clear justification for the popular practice for ingesting long inputs all at once and maintaining long conversational histories as discussed above, we decompose 0 to pose the following research questions: RQ1 Can long-horizon tasks be completed without long contexts? RQ2 Can long-input tasks be completed without long contexts? RQ3 Can long-horizon tasks be completed taking no more than a single action per context? The rest of this paper is aimed at curtly answering these questions. 2 Methodology We use one methodology to answer all research questions posed in Section 1 . 2.1 Definitions The base term “context” is, unfortunately, considerably overloaded in language modelling. Below we outline our working definitions intended to fix the meaning of otherwise vaguely interpreted terms commonly used in the community and relied on throughout this paper. Their numerical boundaries are rough rules of thumb. Inference step. An inference step is one invocation of an LM to produce output. In agentic workflows, it typically coincides with one agent turn of a conversation. Input context. At a given inference step, the input context is the complete sequence of tokens made available to the LM to produce output. It may include system instructions, the task input, prior model outputs, tool results, and any other conversational history. Output context. At a given inference step, the output context is the complete sequence of tokens generated by the LM in the inference step. It may include a thinking trace, tool calls, user-oriented outputs, or other model output artifacts. Context. At a given inference step, the context is the input context, the input context and an associated output context, or the input context and any token space reserved for a possible output context. Context window and context window size. The framework measures the geometric coherence of \textit{anon-vectors}, the differences in hidden states between a concept-specific query and its anonymized paraphrase, and shows that genuine knowledge forms a tight, low-entropy cluster while ignorance forces geometric fragmentation. Across ten instruction-tuned LLMs from three model families, all fragmentation metrics reliably separate known from unknown concepts, and post-unlearning, fragmentation geometry correlates with adversarial recovery across four attack types and five unlearning algorithms, though the direction of that relationship is shown to depend on attack methodology. Furthermore, a layer-resolved analysis reveals that different adversarial mechanisms exploit this geometry at varying depths, with high attack-specific correlations that are invisible to behavioral evaluation. Together, these results constitute a single-phase, attack-free proxy for unlearning robustness that captures aspects of parametric knowledge inaccessible to output-level metrics.
