items.content: The Geometry of Ignorance: Detecting Suppressed Knowledge in LLMs through Activation Fragmentation Adar Peleg * , Dvir Alsheich * , Tomer Ashuach , Avi Mendelson Affiliation: Technion - Israel Institute of Technology * Equal contribution Correspondence: {a.p, dviralsheich, tomerashuach}@campus.technion.ac.il , mendlson@technion.ac.il Abstract Evaluating whether a large language model (LLM) genuinely knows a concept remains a fundamental problem, since behavioral metrics can be fooled by suppression: a model that refuses to answer may still harbor recoverable knowledge. The framework measures the geometric coherence of anon-vectors , the differences in hidden states between a concept-specific query and its anonymized paraphrase, and shows that genuine knowledge forms a tight, low-entropy cluster while ignorance forces geometric fragmentation. Across ten instruction-tuned LLMs from three model families, all fragmentation metrics reliably separate known from unknown concepts, and post-unlearning, fragmentation geometry correlates with adversarial recovery across four attack types and five unlearning algorithms, though the direction of that relationship is shown to depend on attack methodology. Furthermore, a layer-resolved analysis reveals that different adversarial mechanisms exploit this geometry at varying depths, with high attack-specific correlations that are invisible to behavioral evaluation. Together, these results constitute a single-phase, attack-free proxy for unlearning robustness that captures aspects of parametric knowledge inaccessible to output-level metrics. A reference implementation is available at Concept Query ( q i q_{i} ) “Who is Harry Potter?” Anonymized Vectors ( a i ( k ) a_{i}^{(k)} ) “Who is Alex Ryden?” “Who is Marcus Cole?” ⋮ \vdots − - h l ∗ ​ ( q i ) h_{l^{*}}(q_{i}) 1 K ​ ∑ k = 1 K h l ∗ ​ ( a i ( k ) ) \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}h_{l^{*}}(a_{i}^{(k)}) Δ ​ v i \Delta v_{i} Known Concept Origin Coherent Geometry Unknown Concept Origin Fragmented Geometry Figure 1: Activation fragmentation isolates conceptual knowledge. Subtracting the mean hidden state of a cloud of anonymized variants cancels shared linguistic syntax. Plotting the resulting anon-difference vectors ( Δ ​ v i \Delta v_{i} ) from the origin reveals that parametric knowledge manifests as tight, low-entropy covariance clusters of aligned vectors, whereas ignorance forces geometric fragmentation across high-variance directions. 1 Introduction The expansive pre-training of Large Language Models (LLMs) inevitably leads to the memorisation of vast amounts of factual associations Petroni et al. (2019) ; Meng et al. (2023) , raising critical legal, ethical, and safety concerns regarding privacy and the generation of harmful content Carlini et al. (2021) ; Seyitoğlu et al. (2024) . Traditionally, the boundaries of a model’s parametric knowledge have been evaluated through behavioral analysis, relying on surface-level metrics such as question-answering accuracy or token perplexity Lynch et al. (2024) . Behavioral evaluations treat the model as a black box and fail to capture how factual associations are internally stored and retrieved during the forward pass Geva et al. (2023) . This gap is most consequential in the context of machine unlearning, which aims to selectively erase specific concepts without retraining Li et al. (2024) ; Gandikota et al. (2025) ; Ashuach et al. (2026) . Recent representation-level analyses reveal that unlearning interventions often result in the mere suppression or bypassing of knowledge, rather than genuine deletion Xu et al. (2025) ; Lee et al. (2024) ; Schoepf et al. (2026) . Because suppression mechanisms leave the knowledge structurally distinguishable in the parameters Huu-Tien et al. (2025) , it can be reliably recovered by malicious actors through activation steering Seyitoğlu et al. (2024) . Consequently, robust evaluation must shift to fine-grained, intrinsic metrics that can detect suppressed but recoverable knowledge. Recent mechanistic interpretability work has introduced intrinsic probes that bypass generation and measure knowledge directly within intermediate model layers Gottesman and Geva (2024) ; Hong et al. () . However, these metrics remain entangled with prompt syntax, conflating factual knowledge with the linguistic and syntactic structure of the query. Moreover, no single-phase metric reliably predicts whether suppressed knowledge is adversarially recoverable. To address the limitations of both behavioral evaluations and syntax-entangled intrinsic metrics, we build upon the concept of the anon-vector ( Seyitoğlu et al., 2024 ) , defined as the directional shift between the hidden state of a concept-specific query and its identity-stripped paraphrase. We use this to introduce activation fragmentation , a geometric framework that isolates the precise footprint of parametric knowledge using two forward passes per query (no token generation, no iterative optimization). We hypothesize that unknown concepts lack parametric structure: their anon-difference vectors scatter into high-variance, fragmented directions. By contrast, genuine parametric knowledge manifests as a tight, cohesive geometric signature in activation space. Contributions. Our main contributions are as follows: • We propose activation fragmentation , a fine-grained, representation-level metric that leverages anon-vectors to successfully isolate conceptual identity from syntax in intermediate model layers. • We demonstrate empirically that fragmentation metrics distinguish known entities (e.g., Harry Potter) from completely unknown fictitious concepts (e.g., TOFU Maini et al. (2024) ) with robust statistical separability across ten instruction-tuned LLMs from three distinct model families. • A ctivation U niformity S catter S core (AUSS) . We establish that post-unlearning fragmentation serves as a highly accurate, attack-free predictor of elements of unlearning robustness. (e.g. AUSS dispersion metrics predict in-context learning (ICL) recoverability). 2 Background Knowledge in LLM activations. LLMs encode factual associations in their parameters, with feed-forward layers functioning as key-value memories that promote specific concepts into the residual stream Geva et al. (2021) ; Geva et al. (2022) . Intermediate layers carry geometrically richer knowledge representations than the final layer Skean et al. (2025) ; Razzhigaev et al. (2023) . Skean et al. (2025) measure representational compression layer-by-layer via the Rényi-2 Gram-matrix entropy: for any matrix Z ∈ ℝ M × d Z\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d} , K Z = Z ​ Z ⊤ tr ⁡ ( Z ​ Z ⊤ ) S 2 ​ ( Z ) = − log 2 ⁡ tr ⁡ ( K Z 2 ) \begin{array}[]{c}K_{Z}=\frac{ZZ^{\top}}{\operatorname{tr}(ZZ^{\top})}\\ S_{2}(Z)=-\log_{2}\operatorname{tr}\!\left(K_{Z}^{2}\right)\end{array} (1) Lower S 2 S_{2} indicates that the M M vectors concentrate in a smaller subspace (higher representational compression), identifying where factual content is most geometrically concentrated in the hidden space. Applied to the raw query hidden states 𝐇 = { h ℓ ∗ ​ ( q i ) } \mathbf{H}=\{h_{\ell^{*}}(q_{i})\} , this gives the baseline metric Reg S 2 S_{2} ( Skean et al., 2025 ) : Reg S 2 = S 2 ​ ( 𝐇 ) \mathrm{Reg}_{S_{2}}=S_{2}(\mathbf{H}) . Anon-vectors and concept-differential representations. A concept-specific signal can be isolated by contrasting the hidden state of a real query with that of a semantically equivalent but identity-stripped (anonymised) paraphrase. Seyitoğlu et al. (2024) exploit this to mount an activation steering attack : they compute a steering vector as the raw difference between hidden states of a concept query and its anonymised counterpart, then inject it into the residual stream to re-activate suppressed knowledge in an already-unlearned model. The ConceptVectors dataset Hong et al. () likewise demonstrates that named entities encoded in model parameters leave verifiable parametric traces at intermediate layers, and that jailbreak attacks ride along these very directions to bypass unlearning Hong et al. () . Our anon-difference vector Δ ​ v i \Delta v_{i} (Eq. 2 ) builds directly on the anonymisation technique of Seyitoğlu et al. (2024) , averaging over K K variants to stabilise the concept-differential signal. Neither prior work, however, treats the population geometry of a batch of such vectors as a diagnostic metric; that is a contribution of this paper. 3 Method 3.1 Metric Definitions Anon-vectors and Entropy. Let { q i } i = 1 N \{q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} be N N queries about a target concept, and let h ℓ ​ ( ⋅ ) ∈ ℝ d h_{\ell}(\cdot)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be the mean-pooled hidden states at layer ℓ \ell . For each q i q_{i} , we construct K K anonymised variants { a i ( k ) } k = 1 K \{a_{i}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K} . The anon-difference vector at layer ℓ \ell isolates conceptual identity by subtracting the mean anonymised state: Δ ​ v i ​ ( ℓ ) = h ℓ ​ ( q i ) − 1 K ​ ∑ k = 1 K h ℓ ​ ( a i ( k ) ) \Delta v_{i}(\ell)\;=\;h_{\ell}(q_{i})\;-\;\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}h_{\ell}\!\left(a_{i}^{(k)}\right) (2) This requires two forward passes per query in performed experiments (in general K + 1 K{+}1 per query, with K = 1 K{=}1 in experiment sections) and no token generation. All fragmentation metrics are computed from the matrix of anon-difference vectors at a chosen layer; how that layer is selected is stated in each experimental protocol (Section 4 ) and expended in (Appendix B.3 ). To measure representational rank concentration, we apply Gram-matrix entropy to these unnormalised vectors, defining our primary dispersion metric: AnonDiff S 2 = S 2 ​ ( Δ ​ 𝐕 ​ ( ℓ ) ) \mathrm{AnonDiff}_{S_{2}}=S_{2}(\Delta\mathbf{V}(\ell)) . Applying S 2 S_{2} to concept-differential vectors rather than raw activations is a novel contribution of this work. We also evaluate two variants: Reg S 2 = S 2 ​ ( 𝐇 ℓ ) \mathrm{Reg}_{S_{2}}=S_{2}(\mathbf{H}^{\ell}) applies the same entropy to the raw hidden-state matrix (no anonymisation subtraction), serving as a baseline; and NormAnonDiff S 2 = S 2 ​ ( Δ ^ ​ 𝐕 ​ ( ℓ ) ) \mathrm{NormAnonDiff}_{S_{2}}=S_{2}(\hat{\Delta}\mathbf{V}(\ell)) applies it to the L 2 L_{2} -normalised anon-difference vectors. AUSS Batch-mean metrics (Ours) . To assess population-level geometric consistency, we partition the N N pairs into B = 10 B=10 disjoint batches (Appendix B.3 ). For each batch b b , we compute the unit-normalised mean anon-difference direction d ^ b \hat{d}_{b} . We then measure geometric consistency across these B B representative directions using two primary novel matrices that aim to measure fragmentation : • 𝐀𝐔𝐒𝐒 𝐋 𝟐 \mathbf{AUSS_{L_{2}}} : Mean pairwise squared L 2 L_{2} distance between batch-mean directions. • 𝐀𝐔𝐒𝐒 cos 𝟐 \mathbf{AUSS_{\cos^{2}}} : Complement of mean pairwise squared cosine between batch-mean directions. • 𝐀𝐔𝐒𝐒 𝐉𝐚𝐜 \mathbf{AUSS_{Jac}} : Jaccard distance between the sets of the k = 32 k{=}32 largest-magnitude coordinates of each pair of batch-mean directions, the fraction of top-activated dimensions that differ between batches. Note that all three metrics are bounded: AUSS L 2 ∈ [ 0 , 2 ] \mathrm{AUSS}_{L_{2}}\in[0,2] and AUSS cos 2 , AUSS J ​ a ​ c ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \mathrm{AUSS}_{\cos^{2}},\mathrm{AUSS}_{Jac}\in[0,1] . We expect that when a concept is known, batch-mean directions cluster tightly, driving all three metrics toward zero; when unknown, they are expected to scatter, driving them toward the upper bound. This bounded range means that Cohen’s | d | |d| can appear large even with modest raw gaps, because the pooled within-group standard deviation is bounded from above. A comprehensive list of additionally evaluated metric variations including base pairwise similarities, Jaccard incoherence, and covariance traces is detailed in Appendix C . 3.2 Entropy, Rank, and the Geometry of Parametric Knowledge The central hypothesis of this work is that parametric knowledge leaves a geometric imprint. If a model knows a concept, diverse queries converge onto a shared subspace, producing a tight, low-entropy cluster of anon-difference vectors. Conversely, ignorance drives these vectors to scatter across the activation space, increasing entropy. This connection between the Gram-matrix entropy S 2 S_{2} and geometric dispersion is formalised by the following result (for proofs see Appendix A ): Theorem 1 (High entropy forces geometric fragmentation) . Let A ∈ ℝ n × d A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} be a matrix of L 2 L_{2} -normalised activation vectors and let G = A ​ A ⊤ G=AA^{\top} be the corresponding Gram matrix 1 1 1 For a matrix A A of unit-normalised vectors, the Gram matrix G = A ​ A ⊤ G{=}AA^{\top} collects every pairwise cosine similarity ( G i ​ j = cos ⁡ ( a i , a j ) G_{ij}{=}\cos(a_{i},a_{j}) ), so its eigenvalue spectrum summarises how many effective directions the vectors collectively occupy. with effective rank EffRank ⁡ ( G ) = Tr ⁡ ( G ) / λ max ​ ( G ) \mathrm{EffRank}(G)=\mathrm{Tr}(G)/\lambda_{\max}(G) . Then the mean pairwise squared Euclidean distance satisfies D L 2 2 ≥ 2 − 2 EffRank ⁡ ( G ) . D_{L_{2}}^{2}\;\geq\;2-\frac{2}{\mathrm{EffRank}(G)}. Since 2 S 2 / 2 ≤ EffRank ⁡ ( G ) ≤ 2 S 2 2^{S_{2}/2}\leq\mathrm{EffRank}(G)\leq 2^{S_{2}} (Proposition 1 , Appendix A ), high S 2 S_{2} forces the effective rank upward, which structurally guarantees spatial dispersion. The complementary direction holds under a natural assumption: when all pairwise cosine similarities are non-negative (i.e., vectors share a common half-space). For anon-vectors this is geometrically motivated: if a model parametrically encodes a concept, every query about that concept shifts the hidden state toward the same concept direction , so the differences Δ ​ v i \Delta v_{i} collectively point away from the anonymised baseline in a consistent orientation. Under this assumption, a matching upper bound applies: Theorem 2 (Low entropy forces geometric clustering) . Under the same setup as Theorem 1 , if additionally G i ​ j ≥ 0 G_{ij}\geq 0 for all i ≠ j i\neq j , then D L 2 2 ≤ 2 ​ n n − 1 ​ ( 1 − 2 − S 2 ​ ( G ) ) . D_{L_{2}}^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{2n}{n-1}\!\left(1-2^{-S_{2}(G)}\right). In particular, D L 2 2 → 0 D_{L_{2}}^{2}\to 0 as S 2 ​ ( G ) → 0 S_{2}(G)\to 0 . Together, these bounds demonstrate that subspace-compression metrics directly reflect the presence or absence of a coherent concept representation, effectively isolating knowledge from mere behavioural suppression. 3.3 Semantic Testing Anon-vectors over raw activations. Raw activations encode both conceptual content and prompt syntax. Subtracting the anonymised baseline (denoted as Δ ​ v i \Delta v_{i} ) cancels shared syntactic components, isolating the conceptual signal. This produces a substantially stronger discriminative signal than working with raw activations directly (Table 1 ). Semantic vs. generation artifacts. Behavioral evaluations measure accessible outputs, not latent storage. Since representational suppression mechanisms can block factual recall without deleting the underlying knowledge ( Lee et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) , evaluating hidden-state geometry provides a strictly more rigorous proxy for true parametric erasure. A model that refuses to answer, whether through RLHF-driven refusal or explicit unlearning, may still harbor recoverable knowledge in its hidden states; generation-based metrics will report success while the knowledge persists, making them insufficient as a sole evaluation criteria. The measurement problem: no true oracle. The ideal ground truth for a knowledge-detection metric would be a model trained from scratch on a corpus that provably excludes the target concept, making its ignorance logically certain. In practice, this is prohibitively expensive and inaccessible: controlled pre-training runs require substantial compute, carefully curated multi-billion-token datasets, and institutional resources. There is, therefore, no true oracle for parametric knowledge. We cannot directly observe what a model knows, only what it outputs, and output-level proxies risk circularity when used to calibrate the very metrics designed to go beyond them. Bogus data as a proxy for not knowing. We sidestep this measurement problem by grounding knowledge in dataset construction rather than model training. As the negative class, we draw from data. For example, the TOFU benchmark ( Maini et al., 2024 ) consists entirely of fictitious authors invented for the benchmark and absent from any pre-training corpus. Because these entities were never written about anywhere, no model can have parametric knowledge of them, and there is no plausible mechanism by which such knowledge could exist. As the positive class, we can draw from Harry Potter (HP) QA pairs; HP knowledge is confirmed to persist in the parameters of most LLMs as a consequence of large-scale pre-training ( Carlini et al., 2021 ; Seyitoğlu et al., 2024 ) . A metric that separates HP from TOFU under this protocol has therefore demonstrated genuine knowledge detection, not behavioral correlation. The specific datasets and model counts used in our evaluation are described in Section 4 . 4 Experiments 1. RQ1: How can we measure the binary existence of knowledge in LLMs? Can we suggest a metric that maximizes separation between known and unknown data? 2. RQ2: How can we measure fine-grained knowledge extraction ability from LLMs? items.raw_text: The Geometry of Ignorance: Detecting Suppressed Knowledge in LLMs through Activation Fragmentation Adar Peleg * , Dvir Alsheich * , Tomer Ashuach , Avi Mendelson Affiliation: Technion - Israel Institute of Technology * Equal contribution Correspondence: {a.p, dviralsheich, tomerashuach}@campus.technion.ac.il , mendlson@technion.ac.il Abstract Evaluating whether a large language model (LLM) genuinely knows a concept remains a fundamental problem, since behavioral metrics can be fooled by suppression: a model that refuses to answer may still harbor recoverable knowledge. The framework measures the geometric coherence of anon-vectors , the differences in hidden states between a concept-specific query and its anonymized paraphrase, and shows that genuine knowledge forms a tight, low-entropy cluster while ignorance forces geometric fragmentation. Across ten instruction-tuned LLMs from three model families, all fragmentation metrics reliably separate known from unknown concepts, and post-unlearning, fragmentation geometry correlates with adversarial recovery across four attack types and five unlearning algorithms, though the direction of that relationship is shown to depend on attack methodology. Furthermore, a layer-resolved analysis reveals that different adversarial mechanisms exploit this geometry at varying depths, with high attack-specific correlations that are invisible to behavioral evaluation. Together, these results constitute a single-phase, attack-free proxy for unlearning robustness that captures aspects of parametric knowledge inaccessible to output-level metrics. Subtracting the mean hidden state of a cloud of anonymized variants cancels shared linguistic syntax. Plotting the resulting anon-difference vectors ( Δ ​ v i \Delta v_{i} ) from the origin reveals that parametric knowledge manifests as tight, low-entropy covariance clusters of aligned vectors, whereas ignorance forces geometric fragmentation across high-variance directions. 1 Introduction The expansive pre-training of Large Language Models (LLMs) inevitably leads to the memorisation of vast amounts of factual associations Petroni et al. (2019) ; Meng et al. (2023) , raising critical legal, ethical, and safety concerns regarding privacy and the generation of harmful content Carlini et al. (2021) ; Seyitoğlu et al. (2024) . Traditionally, the boundaries of a model’s parametric knowledge have been evaluated through behavioral analysis, relying on surface-level metrics such as question-answering accuracy or token perplexity Lynch et al. (2024) . Behavioral evaluations treat the model as a black box and fail to capture how factual associations are internally stored and retrieved during the forward pass Geva et al. (2023) . This gap is most consequential in the context of machine unlearning, which aims to selectively erase specific concepts without retraining Li et al. (2024) ; Gandikota et al. (2025) ; Ashuach et al. (2026) . Recent representation-level analyses reveal that unlearning interventions often result in the mere suppression or bypassing of knowledge, rather than genuine deletion Xu et al. (2025) ; Lee et al. (2024) ; Schoepf et al. (2026) . Because suppression mechanisms leave the knowledge structurally distinguishable in the parameters Huu-Tien et al. (2025) , it can be reliably recovered by malicious actors through activation steering Seyitoğlu et al. (2024) . Consequently, robust evaluation must shift to fine-grained, intrinsic metrics that can detect suppressed but recoverable knowledge. Recent mechanistic interpretability work has introduced intrinsic probes that bypass generation and measure knowledge directly within intermediate model layers Gottesman and Geva (2024) ; Hong et al. () . However, these metrics remain entangled with prompt syntax, conflating factual knowledge with the linguistic and syntactic structure of the query. Moreover, no single-phase metric reliably predicts whether suppressed knowledge is adversarially recoverable. To address the limitations of both behavioral evaluations and syntax-entangled intrinsic metrics, we build upon the concept of the anon-vector ( Seyitoğlu et al., 2024 ) , defined as the directional shift between the hidden state of a concept-specific query and its identity-stripped paraphrase. We use this to introduce activation fragmentation , a geometric framework that isolates the precise footprint of parametric knowledge using two forward passes per query (no token generation, no iterative optimization). We hypothesize that unknown concepts lack parametric structure: their anon-difference vectors scatter into high-variance, fragmented directions. By contrast, genuine parametric knowledge manifests as a tight, cohesive geometric signature in activation space. Contributions. Our main contributions are as follows: • We propose activation fragmentation , a fine-grained, representation-level metric that leverages anon-vectors to successfully isolate conceptual identity from syntax in intermediate model layers. • We demonstrate empirically that fragmentation metrics distinguish known entities (e.g., Harry Potter) from completely unknown fictitious concepts (e.g., TOFU Maini et al. (2024) ) with robust statistical separability across ten instruction-tuned LLMs from three distinct model families. • A ctivation U niformity S catter S core (AUSS) . We establish that post-unlearning fragmentation serves as a highly accurate, attack-free predictor of elements of unlearning robustness. (e.g. AUSS dispersion metrics predict in-context learning (ICL) recoverability). 2 Background Knowledge in LLM activations. LLMs encode factual associations in their parameters, with feed-forward layers functioning as key-value memories that promote specific concepts into the residual stream Geva et al. (2021) ; Geva et al. (2022) . Intermediate layers carry geometrically richer knowledge representations than the final layer Skean et al. (2025) ; Razzhigaev et al. (2023) . Skean et al. Anon-vectors and concept-differential representations. A concept-specific signal can be isolated by contrasting the hidden state of a real query with that of a semantically equivalent but identity-stripped (anonymised) paraphrase. Seyitoğlu et al. (2024) exploit this to mount an activation steering attack : they compute a steering vector as the raw difference between hidden states of a concept query and its anonymised counterpart, then inject it into the residual stream to re-activate suppressed knowledge in an already-unlearned model. Raw activations encode both conceptual content and prompt syntax. Subtracting the anonymised baseline (denoted as Δ ​ v i \Delta v_{i} ) cancels shared syntactic components, isolating the conceptual signal. This produces a substantially stronger discriminative signal than working with raw activations directly (Table 1 ). Semantic vs. generation artifacts. Behavioral evaluations measure accessible outputs, not latent storage. Since representational suppression mechanisms can block factual recall without deleting the underlying knowledge ( Lee et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) , evaluating hidden-state geometry provides a strictly more rigorous proxy for true parametric erasure. A model that refuses to answer, whether through RLHF-driven refusal or explicit unlearning, may still harbor recoverable knowledge in its hidden states; generation-based metrics will report success while the knowledge persists, making them insufficient as a sole evaluation criteria. The measurement problem: no true oracle. The ideal ground truth for a knowledge-detection metric would be a model trained from scratch on a corpus that provably excludes the target concept, making its ignorance logically certain. In practice, this is prohibitively expensive and inaccessible: controlled pre-training runs require substantial compute, carefully curated multi-billion-token datasets, and institutional resources. There is, therefore, no true oracle for parametric knowledge. We cannot directly observe what a model knows, only what it outputs, and output-level proxies risk circularity when used to calibrate the very metrics designed to go beyond them. Bogus data as a proxy for not knowing. We sidestep this measurement problem by grounding knowledge in dataset construction rather than model training. As the negative class, we draw from data. For example, the TOFU benchmark ( Maini et al., 2024 ) consists entirely of fictitious authors invented for the benchmark and absent from any pre-training corpus. Because these entities were never written about anywhere, no model can have parametric knowledge of them, and there is no plausible mechanism by which such knowledge could exist. As the positive class, we can draw from Harry Potter (HP) QA pairs; HP knowledge is confirmed to persist in the parameters of most LLMs as a consequence of large-scale pre-training ( Carlini et al., 2021 ; Seyitoğlu et al., 2024 ) . A metric that separates HP from TOFU under this protocol has therefore demonstrated genuine knowledge detection, not behavioral correlation. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.05263 (cs) [Submitted on 3 Nov 2026] Title: JHiMA-WebRL: A Joint Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Long-Horizon Web Tasks Authors: Shanka Subhra Mondal , Jiayun Wang View a PDF of the paper titled JHiMA-WebRL: A Joint Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Long-Horizon Web Tasks, by Shanka Subhra Mondal and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Multimodal web agents have shown promising capabilities for interacting with websites through graphical user interfaces (GUIs), yet realistic web tasks often require long-horizon, multi-step planning that remains challenging for monolithic policies. Such agents must jointly infer high-level plans, navigate through intermediate states, track progress over extended interaction histories, and execute visually grounded actions. Although prior work has explored modular multi-agent systems with a separate planner, the planner is typically not updated jointly with the actor. We investigate whether explicitly separating and jointly training planning and execution provides a stronger inductive bias for long-horizon web navigation. We introduce JHiMA-WebRL, a joint hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for web agents that couples a task decomposer with an actor. To train the decomposer, we use a strong teacher model to construct structured subtask supervision from multimodal GUI trajectories, and use these annotations to fine-tune both the decomposer and the subtask-conditioned actor. We then extend Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to jointly optimize the decomposer and actor in the interactive WebArena environment through hierarchical rollout grouping and role-specific advantages. On WebArena-Lite-v2, JHiMA-WebRL-14B, consisting of a 7B actor and a 7B decomposer, achieves an average success rate of 37.2%, compared with 24% for a ScaleCUA-32B agent that we fine-tune with RL on the same training tasks and evaluate under the same protocol. Ablations show that jointly updating the decomposer during RL outperforms updating the actor alone. These results suggest that jointly learned role factorization with smaller models can be a competitive alternative to scaling monolithic agents for long-horizon web tasks. items.content: JHiMA-WebRL: A Joint Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Long-Horizon Web Tasks Shanka Subhra Mondal Jiayun Wang Affiliation: Center for Advanced AI, Accenture Abstract Multimodal web agents have shown promising capabilities for interacting with websites through graphical user interfaces (GUIs), yet realistic web tasks often require long-horizon, multi-step planning that remains challenging for monolithic policies. Such agents must jointly infer high-level plans, navigate through intermediate states, track progress over extended interaction histories, and execute visually grounded actions. Although prior work has explored modular multi-agent systems with a separate planner, the planner is typically not updated jointly with the actor. We investigate whether explicitly separating and jointly training planning and execution provides a stronger inductive bias for long-horizon web navigation. We introduce JHiMA-WebRL, a joint hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for web agents that couples a task decomposer with an actor. To train the decomposer, we use a strong teacher model to construct structured subtask supervision from multimodal GUI trajectories, and use these annotations to fine-tune both the decomposer and the subtask-conditioned actor. We then extend Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to jointly optimize the decomposer and actor in the interactive WebArena environment through hierarchical rollout grouping and role-specific advantages. On WebArena-Lite-v2, JHiMA-WebRL-14B, consisting of a 7B actor and a 7B decomposer, achieves an average success rate of 37.2%, compared with 24.0% for a ScaleCUA-32B agent that we fine-tune with RL on the same training tasks and evaluate under the same protocol. Ablations show that jointly updating the decomposer during RL outperforms updating the actor alone. These results suggest that jointly learned role factorization with smaller models can be a competitive alternative to scaling monolithic agents for long-horizon web tasks. Figure 1: Overview of JHiMA-WebRL. Left: prior web agents use a single policy, or a separate planner that receives no RL updates while the actor is trained. Right: we generate subtask supervision from GUI trajectories, fine-tune the decomposer and actor, and jointly optimize both with hierarchical RL: K K decompositions, M M actor rollouts each, and role-specific advantages from terminal rewards. 1 Introduction Multimodal web agents interact with websites by perceiving screenshots, interpreting page elements, and executing actions such as clicking, typing, scrolling, and navigating between webpages. Such agents could support workflows in online shopping, web-based administration, repository management, and information retrieval. Benchmarks such as WebArena ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) and VisualWebArena ( Koh et al., 2024 ) evaluate this setting through tasks that require interactive execution across multiple steps. These tasks combine high-level planning with low-level visually grounded control: for example, to cancel an order, an agent must navigate intermediate pages, identify relevant interface elements, track progress over a long action history, and avoid repeated or irrelevant actions. Many web agents use a monolithic policy that maps the task, observation, and action history directly to the next action, learning planning, state tracking, visual grounding, and execution within a single model. ScaleCUA ( Liu et al., 2025b ) and UI-TARS ( Qin et al., 2025 ) demonstrate the value of large-scale GUI data for training such policies, while WebAgent-R1 ( Wei et al., 2025 ) and WebRL ( Qi et al., 2025 ) improve web interaction through online reinforcement learning (RL). Modular systems instead introduce a separate planner: Agent S uses a manager to generate subtasks from retrieved knowledge and experience for workers to execute ( Agashe et al., 2025a ) , and Agent S2 adds proactive replanning as execution provides new observations ( Agashe et al., 2025b ) . Even though an explicit planner module can support long-horizon behavior, the planner’s parameters are not updated from the outcomes of action execution. Recent studies ( Erdogan et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Kong et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) focus on training modular agents for long-horizon tasks, but either train the modules separately, apply supervised learning or RL to only one module while freezing the other, or alternate updates between modules. To our knowledge, prior work has not studied simultaneous RL training of a separately parameterized planner and actor from a shared rollout batch in web environments. We therefore introduce JHiMA-WebRL, a joint hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for long-horizon web interaction. Figure 1 presents an overview of the three stages in our framework: decomposer data generation, supervised fine-tuning, and joint hierarchical multi-agent RL. First, a strong teacher model converts multimodal GUI trajectories into ordered subtasks, supplying planning annotations that existing GUI trajectory datasets typically lack. Second, these annotations support supervised fine-tuning of two Qwen2.5-VL-7B models: a decomposer that predicts subtasks from the instruction and starting screenshot, and an actor that predicts the next GUI action conditioned on those subtasks. Finally, we jointly train both modules using terminal task success rewards while interacting with web environments, so that the decomposer can adapt its plans to the actor’s capabilities while the actor adapts to executing them. We extend Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) through the hierarchical rollout structure: the decomposer proposes K K candidate decompositions, and the actor performs M M complete environment rollouts for each decomposition. Actor-level advantages compare executions under the same plan, while decomposer-level advantages compare plans by the average terminal reward of their executions, and both policies are updated from this shared batch without dense process rewards. We evaluate JHiMA-WebRL-14B, our instantiation with a 7B actor and a 7B decomposer, on WebArena-Lite-v2 ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , a refined subset of WebArena tasks for purely visual agents. JHiMA-WebRL-14B achieves an average success rate of 37.2%, compared with 24.0% for a ScaleCUA-32B agent that we fine-tune with RL on the same training tasks and evaluate under the same protocol. Ablation studies further indicate that jointly updating the decomposer during RL is beneficial relative to updating the actor alone. These results suggest that joint training of role-factorized modules can be a competitive alternative to scaling monolithic agents. 2 Related Work WebArena, VisualWebArena, and WorkArena evaluate agents on web tasks requiring multi-step interaction, visual grounding, state tracking, and long-horizon planning ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Koh et al., 2024 ; Drouin et al., 2024 ) . OSWorld, Windows Agent Arena, and MacArena study the broader setting of desktop and OS-level computer use ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Bonatti et al., 2025 ; Muryn et al., 2026 ) . Strong GUI agents such as UI-TARS and ScaleCUA train largely monolithic policies that map observations and histories directly to actions using large-scale GUI data ( Qin et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) . These systems demonstrate the importance of data scale and GUI grounding, but require a single policy to learn planning, progress tracking, grounding, and execution jointly, whereas we factorize web interaction into a trainable decomposer and actor. A broad line of work studies modular or multi-agent LLM systems, including AutoGen, CAMEL, ChatDev, MetaGPT, and MAP ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Qian et al., 2024 ; Hong et al., 2024 ; Webb et al., 2025 ) . In computer use, Agent S combines manager–worker decomposition with retrieved experience, and Agent S2 updates plans as subtasks are completed ( Agashe et al., 2025a ; Agashe et al., 2025b ) . OpAgent coordinates a planner, grounder, reflector, and summarizer, with the reflector’s feedback guiding subsequent planning ( Guo et al., 2026 ) . These mechanisms concern the organization and adaptation of inference-time behavior. Related methods such as ReAct, Reflexion, MiRA, SEAgent, and TreeCUA explore intermediate reasoning, subgoals, feedback, or structured exploration ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . JHiMA-WebRL focuses on learning the decomposition interface from annotated trajectories and jointly adapting it with the actor through task rewards. A complementary line of work studies training across planner–executor interfaces. Plan-and-Act separately fine-tunes planner and executor models using synthetic plans and action trajectories, and adds dynamic replanning at inference time ( Erdogan et al., 2025 ) . Our approach also uses trajectory-derived planning supervision, then jointly adapts both modules through RL. Navigating WebAI pairs a supervised hierarchical planner with an RL-trained controller ( Thil et al., 2024 ) . Planner Matters! optimizes only the planner using trajectory rewards from a VLM judge, freezing the actor and memory manager ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . Its joint-training ablation shares parameters across roles, whereas our decomposer and actor are separate policies. In robotic manipulation, HiRoC aligns an executor with subgoals through supervised fine-tuning, then applies hierarchical GRPO to the executor with a frozen planner, combining task-level and subgoal-level advantages ( Kong et al., 2026 ) . SWIRL instead trains both modules through alternating RL phases ( Lu et al., 2025 ) . In contrast, JHiMA-WebRL computes actor advantages within plans and decomposer advantages across plans, and updates both policies from a shared rollout batch. PPO and GRPO provide the basic optimization tools for recent LLM and agent RL, while multi-agent RL methods such as MADDPG, COMA, QMIX, and MAPPO study credit assignment across interacting policies ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Shao et al., 2024 ; Lowe et al., 2017 ; Foerster et al., 2018 ; Rashid et al., 2018 ; Yu et al., 2022 ) . For web and GUI agents, WebAgent-R1, WebRL, OpenWebRL, and OpAgent apply online multi-turn RL to browser-based tasks, optimizing a single agent policy from terminal or outcome-based rewards ( Wei et al., 2025 ; Qi et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Guo et al., 2026 ) , while WorkForceAgent-R1 applies rule-based RL to single-step web decisions ( Zhuang et al., 2025 ) . Other works improve credit assignment with process or progress signals, including Web-Shepherd, WebArbiter, TGPO, GraphGPO, and MiRA ( Chae et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . We instead extend GRPO’s rollout grouping and advantage computation to two jointly trained roles, using only terminal rewards and no dense process rewards. 3 Method We propose JHiMA-WebRL, a joint hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for long-horizon web navigation. Our approach factorizes interaction into two specialized but jointly optimized modules: a task decomposer and an actor. The decomposer maps the task instruction and initial screenshot into an ordered sequence of executable subtasks. The actor then conditions on the task, current observation, interaction history, and generated subtasks to produce visually grounded actions in the web interface. Below, we first describe the problem formulation, followed by the three stages of our framework: data generation for training the decomposer, supervised fine-tuning of both the decomposer and actor, and a joint hierarchical multi-agent extension of GRPO. 3.1 Problem Formulation We consider an interactive web environment modeled as a partially observed sequential decision problem. Each task is specified by a natural-language instruction x x . At time step t t , the agent receives a screenshot o t o_{t} of the web interface and produces an action a t ∈ 𝒜 a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} , such as clicking a page element, typing, scrolling, navigating between webpages, or terminating with an answer. The environment then transitions to a new state and returns the next observation o t + 1 o_{t+1} . A trajectory is denoted by τ = ( o 0 , a 0 , o 1 , a 1 , … , o T ) \tau=(o_{0},a_{0},o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{T}) , where T T is the trajectory length. Each trajectory receives a terminal task reward R ⁡ ( τ ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } R(\tau)\in\{0,1\} , where R ⁡ ( τ ) = 1 R(\tau)=1 if the task is successfully completed and R ⁡ ( τ ) = 0 R(\tau)=0 otherwise. Success is determined through environment-specific rule-based verification or an LLM judge. Our modular policy consists of a decomposer policy π D ≡ π θ D \pi_{D}\equiv\pi_{\theta_{D}} and an actor policy π A ≡ π θ A \pi_{A}\equiv\pi_{\theta_{A}} , parameterized by separate models. Given a task instruction x x and an initial observation o 0 o_{0} , the decomposer samples a decomposition d = ( g 1 , g 2 , … , g L ) ∼ π D ( ⋅ ∣ x , o 0 ) , d=(g_{1},g_{2},\ldots,g_{L})\sim\pi_{D}(\cdot\mid x,o_{0}), (1) where each g ℓ g_{\ell} is a natural-language subtask and L L is the number of generated subtasks. The actor then generates web-interface actions according to a t ∼ π A ( ⋅ ∣ x , o t , h t , d ) , a_{t}\sim\pi_{A}(\cdot\mid x,o_{t},h_{t},d), (2) where h t = ( a 0 , … , a t − 1 ) h_{t}=(a_{0},\ldots,a_{t-1}) denotes the action history. 3.2 Decomposer Data Generation Existing GUI trajectory datasets contain task instructions, screenshots, and action traces, but typically do not provide explicit subtask annotations. To train a task decomposer, we construct a new decomposition dataset from trajectory annotations in ScaleCUA ( Liu et al., 2025b ) . ScaleCUA provides large-scale multimodal GUI data across platforms, including grounding annotations and human or agent trajectories. For each trajectory, we provide a strong teacher model, GPT-5.2-Codex ( OpenAI, 2025 ) , with the original task instruction x x and starting screenshot o 0 o_{0} , together with the full sequence of user or agent actions ( a 0 , … , a T − 1 ) (a_{0},\ldots,a_{T-1}) and corresponding screenshots ( o 0 , … , o T ) (o_{0},\ldots,o_{T}) . A subgoal-generation guideline prompt, included in Appendix A , guides the annotation process. The teacher produces an ordered list of executable subtasks d = ( g 1 , … , g L ) d=(g_{1},\ldots,g_{L}) and optional descriptions of unnecessary or redundant actions in the trajectory. This process yields approximately 76 76 K decomposer training examples; dataset statistics are provided in Table 3 , and qualitative examples are shown in Appendix C . The resulting automated pipeline converts low-level multimodal GUI demonstrations into high-level planning supervision, enabling us to train an open-source decomposer rather than relying on a proprietary teacher at inference time. 3.3 Supervised Fine-Tuning We first train both modules with supervised fine-tuning before reinforcement learning. Decomposer SFT. The decomposer is initialized from the Qwen2.5-VL-7B model and trained on the generated subtask dataset. items.raw_text: JHiMA-WebRL: A Joint Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Long-Horizon Web Tasks Shanka Subhra Mondal Jiayun Wang Affiliation: Center for Advanced AI, Accenture Abstract Multimodal web agents have shown promising capabilities for interacting with websites through graphical user interfaces (GUIs), yet realistic web tasks often require long-horizon, multi-step planning that remains challenging for monolithic policies. Such agents must jointly infer high-level plans, navigate through intermediate states, track progress over extended interaction histories, and execute visually grounded actions. Although prior work has explored modular multi-agent systems with a separate planner, the planner is typically not updated jointly with the actor. We investigate whether explicitly separating and jointly training planning and execution provides a stronger inductive bias for long-horizon web navigation. We introduce JHiMA-WebRL, a joint hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for web agents that couples a task decomposer with an actor. To train the decomposer, we use a strong teacher model to construct structured subtask supervision from multimodal GUI trajectories, and use these annotations to fine-tune both the decomposer and the subtask-conditioned actor. We then extend Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to jointly optimize the decomposer and actor in the interactive WebArena environment through hierarchical rollout grouping and role-specific advantages. On WebArena-Lite-v2, JHiMA-WebRL-14B, consisting of a 7B actor and a 7B decomposer, achieves an average success rate of 37.2%, compared with 24.0% for a ScaleCUA-32B agent that we fine-tune with RL on the same training tasks and evaluate under the same protocol. Ablations show that jointly updating the decomposer during RL outperforms updating the actor alone. These results suggest that jointly learned role factorization with smaller models can be a competitive alternative to scaling monolithic agents for long-horizon web tasks. Figure 1: Overview of JHiMA-WebRL. Left: prior web agents use a single policy, or a separate planner that receives no RL updates while the actor is trained. Right: we generate subtask supervision from GUI trajectories, fine-tune the decomposer and actor, and jointly optimize both with hierarchical RL: K K decompositions, M M actor rollouts each, and role-specific advantages from terminal rewards. 1 Introduction Multimodal web agents interact with websites by perceiving screenshots, interpreting page elements, and executing actions such as clicking, typing, scrolling, and navigating between webpages. Such agents could support workflows in online shopping, web-based administration, repository management, and information retrieval. Benchmarks such as WebArena ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) and VisualWebArena ( Koh et al., 2024 ) evaluate this setting through tasks that require interactive execution across multiple steps. These tasks combine high-level planning with low-level visually grounded control: for example, to cancel an order, an agent must navigate intermediate pages, identify relevant interface elements, track progress over a long action history, and avoid repeated or irrelevant actions. Many web agents use a monolithic policy that maps the task, observation, and action history directly to the next action, learning planning, state tracking, visual grounding, and execution within a single model. ScaleCUA ( Liu et al., 2025b ) and UI-TARS ( Qin et al., 2025 ) demonstrate the value of large-scale GUI data for training such policies, while WebAgent-R1 ( Wei et al., 2025 ) and WebRL ( Qi et al., 2025 ) improve web interaction through online reinforcement learning (RL). Modular systems instead introduce a separate planner: Agent S uses a manager to generate subtasks from retrieved knowledge and experience for workers to execute ( Agashe et al., 2025a ) , and Agent S2 adds proactive replanning as execution provides new observations ( Agashe et al., 2025b ) . Even though an explicit planner module can support long-horizon behavior, the planner’s parameters are not updated from the outcomes of action execution. Recent studies ( Erdogan et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Kong et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) focus on training modular agents for long-horizon tasks, but either train the modules separately, apply supervised learning or RL to only one module while freezing the other, or alternate updates between modules. To our knowledge, prior work has not studied simultaneous RL training of a separately parameterized planner and actor from a shared rollout batch in web environments. We therefore introduce JHiMA-WebRL, a joint hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for long-horizon web interaction. Figure 1 presents an overview of the three stages in our framework: decomposer data generation, supervised fine-tuning, and joint hierarchical multi-agent RL. First, a strong teacher model converts multimodal GUI trajectories into ordered subtasks, supplying planning annotations that existing GUI trajectory datasets typically lack. Second, these annotations support supervised fine-tuning of two Qwen2.5-VL-7B models: a decomposer that predicts subtasks from the instruction and starting screenshot, and an actor that predicts the next GUI action conditioned on those subtasks. Finally, we jointly train both modules using terminal task success rewards while interacting with web environments, so that the decomposer can adapt its plans to the actor’s capabilities while the actor adapts to executing them. We extend Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) through the hierarchical rollout structure: the decomposer proposes K K candidate decompositions, and the actor performs M M complete environment rollouts for each decomposition. Actor-level advantages compare executions under the same plan, while decomposer-level advantages compare plans by the average terminal reward of their executions, and both policies are updated from this shared batch without dense process rewards. We evaluate JHiMA-WebRL-14B, our instantiation with a 7B actor and a 7B decomposer, on WebArena-Lite-v2 ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , a refined subset of WebArena tasks for purely visual agents. JHiMA-WebRL-14B achieves an average success rate of 37.2%, compared with 24.0% for a ScaleCUA-32B agent that we fine-tune with RL on the same training tasks and evaluate under the same protocol. Ablation studies further indicate that jointly updating the decomposer during RL is beneficial relative to updating the actor alone. These results suggest that joint training of role-factorized modules can be a competitive alternative to scaling monolithic agents. 2 Related Work WebArena, VisualWebArena, and WorkArena evaluate agents on web tasks requiring multi-step interaction, visual grounding, state tracking, and long-horizon planning ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Koh et al., 2024 ; Drouin et al., 2024 ) . OSWorld, Windows Agent Arena, and MacArena study the broader setting of desktop and OS-level computer use ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Bonatti et al., 2025 ; Muryn et al., 2026 ) . Strong GUI agents such as UI-TARS and ScaleCUA train largely monolithic policies that map observations and histories directly to actions using large-scale GUI data ( Qin et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) . These systems demonstrate the importance of data scale and GUI grounding, but require a single policy to learn planning, progress tracking, grounding, and execution jointly, whereas we factorize web interaction into a trainable decomposer and actor. A broad line of work studies modular or multi-agent LLM systems, including AutoGen, CAMEL, ChatDev, MetaGPT, and MAP ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Qian et al., 2024 ; Hong et al., 2024 ; Webb et al., 2025 ) . In computer use, Agent S combines manager–worker decomposition with retrieved experience, and Agent S2 updates plans as subtasks are completed ( Agashe et al., 2025a ; Agashe et al., 2025b ) . OpAgent coordinates a planner, grounder, reflector, and summarizer, with the reflector’s feedback guiding subsequent planning ( Guo et al., 2026 ) . These mechanisms concern the organization and adaptation of inference-time behavior. Related methods such as ReAct, Reflexion, MiRA, SEAgent, and TreeCUA explore intermediate reasoning, subgoals, feedback, or structured exploration ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . JHiMA-WebRL focuses on learning the decomposition interface from annotated trajectories and jointly adapting it with the actor through task rewards. A complementary line of work studies training across planner–executor interfaces. Plan-and-Act separately fine-tunes planner and executor models using synthetic plans and action trajectories, and adds dynamic replanning at inference time ( Erdogan et al., 2025 ) . Our approach also uses trajectory-derived planning supervision, then jointly adapts both modules through RL. Navigating WebAI pairs a supervised hierarchical planner with an RL-trained controller ( Thil et al., 2024 ) . Planner Matters! optimizes only the planner using trajectory rewards from a VLM judge, freezing the actor and memory manager ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . Its joint-training ablation shares parameters across roles, whereas our decomposer and actor are separate policies. In robotic manipulation, HiRoC aligns an executor with subgoals through supervised fine-tuning, then applies hierarchical GRPO to the executor with a frozen planner, combining task-level and subgoal-level advantages ( Kong et al., 2026 ) . SWIRL instead trains both modules through alternating RL phases ( Lu et al., 2025 ) . In contrast, JHiMA-WebRL computes actor advantages within plans and decomposer advantages across plans, and updates both policies from a shared rollout batch. PPO and GRPO provide the basic optimization tools for recent LLM and agent RL, while multi-agent RL methods such as MADDPG, COMA, QMIX, and MAPPO study credit assignment across interacting policies ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Shao et al., 2024 ; Lowe et al., 2017 ; Foerster et al., 2018 ; Rashid et al., 2018 ; Yu et al., 2022 ) . For web and GUI agents, WebAgent-R1, WebRL, OpenWebRL, and OpAgent apply online multi-turn RL to browser-based tasks, optimizing a single agent policy from terminal or outcome-based rewards ( Wei et al., 2025 ; Qi et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Guo et al., 2026 ) , while WorkForceAgent-R1 applies rule-based RL to single-step web decisions ( Zhuang et al., 2025 ) . Other works improve credit assignment with process or progress signals, including Web-Shepherd, WebArbiter, TGPO, GraphGPO, and MiRA ( Chae et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . We instead extend GRPO’s rollout grouping and advantage computation to two jointly trained roles, using only terminal rewards and no dense process rewards. 3 Method We propose JHiMA-WebRL, a joint hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for long-horizon web navigation. Our approach factorizes interaction into two specialized but jointly optimized modules: a task decomposer and an actor. The decomposer maps the task instruction and initial screenshot into an ordered sequence of executable subtasks. Note: Current and historical H.15 data, along with weekly, monthly, and annual averages, are available on the Board's Data Download Program (DDP) at www.federalreserve.gov/datadownload/Choose.aspx?rel=H15 ). Weekly, monthly and annual rates are averages of business days unless otherwise noted. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: November 04, 2026 Back to Top
